title: Matthew
subtitle: All Twenty-Eight Chapters - Key Notes, Cross-References, and Prophecy Fulfilled (WEB)

items.value: This book walks through all twenty-eight chapters of Matthew, one chapter at a time, with the full text of every chapter printed in it. It grew out of a series of eight study guides written for a group working through Matthew three chapters a week. Those guides still exist and still work; this is the same material rebuilt as something you can read straight through on your own.
It is a companion to the Jeremiah volume in this series, and it is built the same way. If you have used that one, everything here will be familiar.

The prose is the point. The tables and footnotes are apparatus - useful, and worth using - but they exist to serve a reading of Matthew, not to replace one. If you only ever read the chapter introductions and the scripture text, you will have read this book properly.

One word about what this is not. It is not a commentary in the technical sense, and it does not pretend to settle disputed questions of date, authorship, or the relationship between the Gospels. Where scholars disagree, the disagreement is usually noted and then left alone. What is offered instead is a sustained, attentive reading - the kind of reading you would do out loud, slowly, with people who are willing to stop and ask what a thing actually says.

sections.heading: How this book is put together

items.value: Every chapter follows the same shape.

values: **Key Notes** - the observations worth having in hand before you read: a word that carries more than the translation shows, a custom the first readers took for granted, a connection to something earlier in the book. Each note ends with the verses it comes from.
**Key Cross-References** - eight passages that stand behind or alongside the chapter, grouped by theme.
**Prophecy Fulfilled** - six or seven places where Matthew's own argument runs back into the Hebrew Scriptures. This is the table that makes this Gospel what it is, and it is explained further below.
**For Further Study** - three places to go deeper, from three different traditions.
**Introduction** - the chapter read as a whole before you read it in parts.
**The chapter itself**, printed in full in the World English Bible, with footnote markers on the verses the references belong to.

items.value: Every scripture reference in the book is a live link to the World English Bible on BibleGateway. In the interactive edition, hovering over a footnote marker shows the full text of the passages cited and a line on why they connect, so you can follow a cross-reference without losing your place.

sections.heading: A note on the divine names

items.value: In the notes and introductions this book uses **Yahweh** for the covenant name of God and **Yahshua** for the Messiah, as the group this material was written for does.

The printed scripture text is never altered. The World English Bible renders the covenant name as Yahweh already, and it reads Jesus in the Gospels; both stand exactly as the translators set them. So you will see Yahshua in a paragraph of commentary and Jesus in the verse beneath it. That is deliberate, and it is not a claim that one is a better translation of the Greek. It simply keeps our own speech and the translator's work visibly distinct.

sections.heading: A note on the chapter titles

items.value: The chapter titles in this book are not traditional and are not found in any Bible. They were written for this study - they name what struck us in that chapter rather than summarising it. Nobody should take them as headings the text itself supplies.

sections.heading: Who wrote it, and to whom

items.value: The book never names its author. The title "according to Matthew" was attached early and universally, and the early church was unanimous about it, which is worth something - especially since a tax collector is an odd person to invent as an author for a Gospel.

There is a small internal signature that points the same way. In the list of the twelve in chapter 10, this Gospel alone calls him "Matthew the tax collector." Mark and Luke give the name without the job. Only here does the writer keep the label attached to himself, years later, in his own book.

The audience is easier. This Gospel assumes a reader who knows the Hebrew Scriptures. It quotes them constantly, argues from them, and does not stop to explain Jewish customs the way Mark does - except in a few places where it does, which suggests a mixed congregation with Gentiles in it. It is written to people for whom the question "is this the Messiah the prophets promised?" is the question that matters most.

Matthew is built around five great blocks of teaching, each closed with the same formula - "when Jesus had finished these words." Many readers have seen a deliberate echo of the five books of Moses in that structure.

values: **The Sermon on the Mount** - chapters 5 to 7, closing at 7:28.
**The commissioning of the Twelve** - chapter 10, closing at 11:1.
**The parables of the Kingdom** - chapter 13, closing at 13:53.
**Life together in the assembly** - chapter 18, closing at 19:1.
**The Olivet discourse** - chapters 23 to 25, closing at 26:1.

items.value: Narrative runs between the blocks, and the whole thing is framed: a genealogy and a birth at the front, a death and a resurrection at the back. Two phrases mark the turns of the story - "from that time Jesus began to preach" at 4:17, and "from that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer" at 16:21. Everything after that second phrase is a journey toward one week.

Matthew's distinctive move is the formula quotation: "this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet." He uses it about a dozen times, and the argument behind it runs through the whole book.

The second reference table in every chapter is built on this. In the Jeremiah volume that table traced connections forward, from the prophet to Messiah. Here it runs the other way - back from Matthew into the Scriptures he is reading. That is his own method, and it seemed right to follow it rather than impose the other one.

It is worth saying plainly that Matthew's use of the Hebrew Scriptures is not always the straightforward prediction-and-fulfilment we might expect. Sometimes he quotes a passage whose original setting was not obviously about a coming Messiah at all - Hosea 11:1, "out of Egypt I called my son," is about the exodus. Matthew is doing something more like pattern-reading than proof-texting: Israel's story is being lived through again, properly this time, by one person. Where a quotation works that way, the notes say so.

Matthew says "Kingdom of Heaven" where Mark and Luke say "Kingdom of God." The phrase appears thirty-three times, and it is almost certainly the ordinary Jewish reverence for the divine name at work - heaven standing in for God.

The Kingdom in this Gospel is not a place people go. It is a reign that has arrived in a person, that is resisted, that grows quietly like seed and yeast, that will be publicly established, and that makes demands now on anyone who receives it. Nearly every parable in the book is answering the question of what that reign is like.

Dates offered for Matthew run from the 50s to the 80s of the first century, and the arguments turn largely on chapter 24 - on whether the prediction of the temple's destruction must have been written after AD 70. Readers who take predictive prophecy seriously will not find that argument decisive, and this book does not attempt to settle the question.

What can be said is that the Gospel reads as though the temple is still standing and the argument with the synagogue is still live. It is a book written inside a family quarrel, by someone who believes the family's own Scriptures have been answered.
Read a chapter a sitting if you can. Read the introduction first, then the chapter itself, and come back to the notes and tables afterward - they will mean more once the text is in you.
If you are reading with others, the introductions are written to be read aloud. That is what they were for originally, and they still work best that way.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 1 - The Genealogy, and the Women in the List
chapters.title: The Genealogy, and the Women in the List
keyNotes: Matthew opens with "the book of the genealogy" - biblos geneseos in Greek, the same phrase the Septuagint uses at Genesis 2:4 and 5:1. He is announcing a new beginning, and expects you to hear it (Matthew 1:1).
Two titles sit in the first sentence, and the whole Gospel works them out: son of David, which is the throne, and son of Abraham, which is the promise that all nations would be blessed (Matthew 1:1).
Four women appear in a genealogy that had no obligation to name a single one - Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah (Matthew 1:3-6).

Every one of them carries a scandal, a foreign birth, or both. Tamar posed as a prostitute to get justice from her father-in-law; Rahab was a Canaanite prostitute; Ruth was a Moabite; Bathsheba was taken in adultery (Matthew 1:3-6).
Bathsheba is not named. She is "her who had been Uriah's wife" - a phrasing that keeps David's crime in the record rather than letting the list tidy it away (Matthew 1:6).
The line runs through Jechoniah, the Coniah of Jeremiah 22, over whom God said to write the man childless, with no offspring prospering on David's throne (Matthew 1:11).

Three sets of fourteen, and Matthew says so out loud. Getting there requires leaving three kings out of the middle set, which ancient genealogies did freely - the list is making an argument, not filing a census (Matthew 1:17).
Fourteen is the numeric value of David's name in Hebrew, since D-V-D is 4 + 6 + 4. The shape of the list is itself saying "David" three times (Matthew 1:17).

The chain of "became the father of" runs unbroken for sixteen verses and then stops. Verse 16 does not say Joseph became the father of Jesus; it says Joseph was the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born (Matthew 1:16).
Joseph is called a righteous man in the very act of planning a quiet divorce rather than a public one. Mercy is being counted as righteousness before the angel says anything (Matthew 1:19).
"You shall call his name Jesus" - Yeshua, which means Yahweh saves. The name is the job description (Matthew 1:21).
And what He saves from is named immediately: not Rome, not Herod, but their sins. The first-century expectation is corrected in the first chapter (Matthew 1:21).
Verse 22 is the first of Matthew's formula quotations - "that it might be fulfilled" - a phrase he will use more than any other Gospel writer (Matthew 1:22).
Immanuel, God with us, brackets the whole Gospel. Matthew's last verse is "I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (Matthew 1:23).
Joseph obeys and never says a word. He does not speak anywhere in the New Testament (Matthew 1:24-25).

intro: Almost nobody reads the genealogy. Most readers skip to verse 18, where the story appears to start. But Matthew put seventeen verses of names at the front of his Gospel on purpose, and to skip them is to miss the argument he is making before he tells us anything at all.

Start with the first phrase. "The book of the genealogy" is biblos geneseos in Greek, which is exactly what the Greek Old Testament calls Genesis. Matthew's opening words are the opening words of the Bible. He is not beginning a biography. He is announcing that the story is starting again.

Then watch who he puts in the list. Jewish genealogies traced fathers. Women were not required and were usually absent. Matthew names four, and they are not the four anyone would have chosen. Tamar, who dressed as a prostitute to force her father-in-law to keep his word. Rahab, who actually was one, and a Canaanite. Ruth, a Moabite, from the nation Deuteronomy barred from the assembly. And Bathsheba, who is not even given her name, only "her who had been Uriah's wife," so that David's adultery and the murder that covered it stay attached to the record.

Whatever else that list is, it is not a sanitised one. The King comes through a family that includes deception, prostitution, foreignness and violent scandal, and Matthew declines to clean any of it up. A reader whose own line contains things they would rather not read aloud is looking at the genealogy they belong in.

Jechoniah in verse 11 is worth noticing as well. That is Coniah, the king of Jeremiah 22, of whom Yahweh said: write this man childless, for no man of his offspring will prosper sitting on David's throne. The legal line runs straight through a man under a curse, and this is exactly why verse 16 breaks its own pattern. Sixteen verses of "became the father of" and then, at the end, not that at all: Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom was born Jesus. The Greek relative pronoun there is feminine. The line comes through Mary; the throne comes through Joseph; the curse is stepped around rather than broken.

And then Joseph himself, who is called righteous for the way he plans to end the engagement. He had the legal right to a public accusation. He chose a quiet divorce, to protect a woman he believed had betrayed him. Matthew calls that righteousness before the angel ever appears.
The name is the thing to sit with. He shall save his people from their sins. Not from Rome, which was what everyone was praying about. From the thing they had stopped noticing.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 2 - Wise Men, a Frightened King, and Four Dreams
chapters.title: Wise Men, a Frightened King, and Four Dreams
keyNotes: The magi are not kings, and the text never numbers them. Three gifts are listed; the men are not counted. They were a priestly and astrological class, most likely from Persia or Babylon (Matthew 2:1).
That origin is worth holding: Daniel had been made chief of the wise men of Babylon centuries earlier, and his book carries a timetable for Messiah's coming (Matthew 2:1-2).
Their question assumes the birth was written in the sky, and that a foreign court had been reading (Matthew 2:2).
Herod is troubled, "and all Jerusalem with him." The city that should have run to Bethlehem is unsettled instead (Matthew 2:3).
The chief priests and scribes answer instantly and correctly - Bethlehem, from Micah 5 - which means the information was never the problem (Matthew 2:4-6).
And then nobody goes. Bethlehem is about five miles from Jerusalem. The men who could quote the verse would not walk the distance to look (Matthew 2:5-6).
The magi, who had travelled for months on far less, arrive and fall down and worship (Matthew 2:11).
The gifts are gold, frankincense and myrrh. The text does not interpret them, though myrrh is a strange thing to bring a toddler - it was used for embalming (Matthew 2:11).
By verse 11 the family is in a house and the child is called a young child rather than a baby, so the visit is months, possibly a year or more, after the birth (Matthew 2:11).
Four dreams steer this chapter: the magi warned, Joseph told to flee, Joseph recalled, Joseph diverted to Galilee. God is directing the story while Herod thinks he is (Matthew 2:12-22).
The flight into Egypt runs the exodus backwards. The Son goes down into Egypt and is called out of it (Matthew 2:13-15).
Hosea 11:1, in its own context, is about Israel the nation coming out of Egypt. Matthew reads Messiah as the true Israel, living her history over again and getting it right (Matthew 2:15).

Herod's massacre fits everything Josephus records of him - he executed his own wife and three of his sons. Bethlehem was a village, so the number of boys under two was likely a dozen or so; small enough for Rome not to notice, total for the families involved (Matthew 2:16).
Matthew quotes Jeremiah 31:15, Rachel weeping in Ramah. It is worth knowing what comes next in Jeremiah: refrain your voice from weeping, for your work will be rewarded (Matthew 2:17-18).
"He will be called a Nazarene" matches no single verse in the prophets, and Matthew says "prophets" plural. The likeliest reading is a play on netzer, the branch of Isaiah 11:1 (Matthew 2:23).

intro: Almost everything most people picture about this chapter comes from Christmas cards rather than from Matthew. There are no kings here, and no number of them. There is no stable, no manger, and no night sky over a barn. By verse 11 the family is in a house and the child is called a young child rather than an infant. This visit is months after the birth, possibly more than a year.

What is actually here is stranger and better. Foreign astrologers, probably from Persia or Babylon, read something in the sky and set out on a journey of months. Hold that against Daniel, who was made chief of the wise men of Babylon and left them a book with a timetable in it. Somebody in the east had been keeping records.

They arrive in Jerusalem and ask a perfectly reasonable question, and the city goes cold. Herod is troubled, which for Herod is dangerous, since this is a man who executed his own wife and three of his sons, and all Jerusalem is troubled with him.

Then comes the detail that should stop any reader. Herod asks the chief priests and scribes where Messiah is to be born, and they answer immediately and correctly. Bethlehem. They quote Micah from memory. They know the address.

And not one of them goes. Bethlehem is five miles down the road. Pagan astrologers crossed a desert on a star; the men who could cite chapter and verse would not walk an afternoon to look. It is the sharpest thing in the chapter, and Matthew never comments on it. He simply lets the two groups stand side by side.

The dreams are worth watching too. Four of them, and each one moves the story: the magi are warned off, Joseph is sent to Egypt, Joseph is called back, Joseph is turned aside to Galilee. Herod believes he is running events. He is being routed around.

And notice which verse Matthew reaches for when the soldiers come to Bethlehem. Jeremiah 31:15, Rachel weeping in Ramah, refusing comfort. Anyone who has been through Jeremiah knows what sits in the very next verse: refrain your voice from weeping, for your work will be rewarded, and there is hope for your latter end. Matthew quotes the grief and expects his reader to know the answer that follows it.
The two groups are the thing to hold onto, and it is worth being honest about which one is easier to belong to. Knowing where He is has never been the same thing as going.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 3 - The Voice in the Wilderness and the Fitting Way
chapters.title: The Voice in the Wilderness and the Fitting Way
keyNotes: John appears in the wilderness rather than the temple. It is where Israel was formed, where the law was given, and where God has a long habit of starting again (Matthew 3:1).
His message is seven words: repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand. Yahshua will preach the identical sentence in chapter 4. The forerunner and the King say the same thing (Matthew 3:2).
Matthew writes "Kingdom of Heaven" where Mark and Luke write "Kingdom of God" - a Jewish reverence about pronouncing the Name, not a different kingdom (Matthew 3:2).
Isaiah 40:3 is applied to him: a voice crying, make ready the way. Servants of an approaching king literally went ahead and levelled the road (Matthew 3:3).
John's clothing is a quotation. Camel's hair and a leather belt is how 2 Kings describes Elijah, almost word for word, and Malachi had promised Elijah before the day of Yahweh (Matthew 3:4).
Whole regions come out to him and are baptized, confessing sins (Matthew 3:5-6).

The offence in that is easy to miss. Ritual immersion for Gentiles converting into Israel already existed. John applies it to Jews - telling the covenant people they need what outsiders need (Matthew 3:6).
Pharisees and Sadducees both come, which is remarkable given they agreed on almost nothing, and both get called offspring of vipers (Matthew 3:7).
"Produce fruit worthy of repentance" makes repentance measurable. It is known by what grows out of it, not by what was felt during it (Matthew 3:8).

The security John dismantles is ancestry: do not say we have Abraham for our father. God can raise children to Abraham from these stones - and in Aramaic the words for children and stones are near neighbours (Matthew 3:9).
The axe is laid at the root, not the branches. This is not pruning (Matthew 3:10).
John's water is for repentance; the one coming after baptizes in the Holy Spirit. John rates himself lower than a slave, who at least carried the sandals (Matthew 3:11).
The winnowing fork, the threshing floor, the wheat and the chaff - the same harvest imagery the prophets used, now put in the hand of the one who is coming (Matthew 3:12).
Then Yahshua arrives to be baptized, and John tries to stop Him. The objection is exactly right: the sinless one is asking for the sign of repentance (Matthew 3:13-14).
"This is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness" are the first recorded words of Yahshua in this Gospel, and they are about standing where His people stand (Matthew 3:15).
The whole Godhead is present in one scene - the Son in the water, the Spirit descending, the Father speaking (Matthew 3:16-17).

And the Father's sentence braids two prophecies together: "you are my Son" from Psalm 2, the coronation psalm, and "in whom I am well pleased" from Isaiah 42, the first Servant song. The King and the Suffering Servant named in one breath (Matthew 3:17).

intro: Four hundred years of silence, and then a man in the desert wearing camel's hair.

The clothing is not a costume note. Camel's hair and a leather belt is how 2 Kings describes Elijah, almost word for word, and Malachi, the last voice before the silence, had closed the Old Testament promising Elijah before the great and terrible day. Anyone who knew the scriptures and saw John's outfit knew what was being claimed before he opened his mouth.

And when he opens it he says seven words that Yahshua will repeat, unchanged, in the next chapter. Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand. The forerunner does not have a warm-up message. He has the same message.

Then the baptism, whose shock has worn off with familiarity. Ritual immersion already existed in Israel, for Gentiles converting in. It said: you are coming from outside, and you need washing to enter. John stands in the Jordan and offers that to Jews. He is telling the covenant people that their position is the same as an outsider's.

Which is precisely why he goes after the ancestry argument. Do not say to yourselves, we have Abraham for our father. God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones, and the line is sharper in Aramaic, where the words for sons and for stones sit right next to each other. Pedigree is not the point. God can make family out of gravel.

Then Yahshua walks down to the water, and John does the only sensible thing and tries to stop Him. His objection is theologically perfect. This is a baptism of repentance. You have nothing to repent of. I should be coming to you.

And the answer is the first thing Yahshua says in this Gospel: allow it now, for this is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness. He is not being baptized because He needs it. He is standing in the line with the people who do. The first recorded act of His ministry is to put Himself among sinners at the very point where they admit it.

The last two verses carry the weight. Heaven opens, the Spirit comes down, and the Father speaks, and what He says is stitched from two different prophecies. "You are my Son" is Psalm 2, the coronation of the King. "In whom I am well pleased" is Isaiah 42, the first song of the Suffering Servant. The throne and the cross, named together, before a word has been preached.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 4 - Forty Days, Three Refusals, and Four Men Who Left Their Nets
chapters.title: Forty Days, Three Refusals, and Four Men Who Left Their Nets
keyNotes: The Spirit leads Him into it. This is not an ambush the devil arranged and heaven failed to prevent - the testing is on purpose (Matthew 4:1).
Forty days and forty nights puts three stories on the table at once: Israel's forty years in the wilderness, Moses' forty days on Sinai, and Elijah's forty to Horeb (Matthew 4:2).
Israel was tested in a wilderness and failed. Messiah is tested in a wilderness and does not, which is the argument the whole scene is making (Matthew 4:1-11).
All three of His answers come from Deuteronomy 6 to 8 - the very chapters explaining why Israel was put in the wilderness in the first place (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10).
The tempter opens with "if you are the Son of God," which is the exact thing the voice from heaven had settled eleven verses earlier. The attack is on a word already spoken (Matthew 4:3).
The first test is bread, and it is not really about hunger. It is about whether sonship entitles you to shortcut the Father's provision (Matthew 4:3-4).

In the second test the devil quotes scripture, and quotes it accurately - Psalm 91 - while leaving out the clause "in all your ways." A verse can be reproduced perfectly and still be used to push someone off a building (Matthew 4:6).
The answer names Massah: you shall not test the Lord your God. Demanding that God prove Himself on cue is the oldest form of unbelief there is (Matthew 4:7).
The third offer is every kingdom of the world, and the offer is not empty enough to be harmless - the kingdoms will be His, but by way of a cross rather than a bow (Matthew 4:8-9).
"Get behind me, Satan" are words He will say again in chapter 16, to Peter, when Peter suggests He skip the cross (Matthew 4:10).
The angels come and serve Him afterward, not during. Help arrives on the far side (Matthew 4:11).
His public ministry begins the moment John's ends. He withdraws to Galilee when he hears John has been arrested (Matthew 4:12).
Capernaum sits in Zebulun and Naphtali - the first territories Assyria deported, the part of the country longest in the dark. That is where the light is switched on (Matthew 4:13-16).
His opening sermon is John's sermon, word for word: repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand (Matthew 4:17).
The call reverses the custom. Students sought out a rabbi; here the Rabbi walks the shoreline and picks working men off their boats (Matthew 4:18-19).
"Fishers for men" is not a fresh metaphor. Jeremiah 16 has fishers sent out to gather a scattered people (Matthew 4:19).
Twice the text says immediately. The first pair leave their nets; the second leave the boat and their father in it (Matthew 4:20-22).
Verse 23 sums the ministry in three verbs - teaching, preaching, healing - and Matthew repeats the same sentence in chapter 9 to bracket everything between (Matthew 4:23).

intro: Notice who does the leading. Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. This is not an ambush that heaven failed to see coming. The Spirit that descended like a dove twelve verses ago walks Him straight into it.

And the arithmetic is deliberate. Forty days in a wilderness is Israel's forty years compressed into one man's fast. Israel was taken into the desert to be humbled and tested, to find out what was in her heart, and she failed on bread, on water, and on a golden calf. The three temptations are about bread, testing God, and worship. The same three, in the same wilderness, with the opposite result.

Then watch where every answer comes from. Deuteronomy 8, Deuteronomy 6, Deuteronomy 6 again, the chapters that explain the wilderness. He is not reaching for whatever verse comes to mind. He is answering out of the passage that is actually about the situation He is standing in.

The second temptation is the one worth slowing down on, because the devil quotes scripture and quotes it correctly. Psalm 91, on the angels bearing you up. What he leaves out is three words, "in all your ways," which is the difference between God's protection over a life being lived and a stunt. Scripture can be reproduced accurately and still be used to talk someone off a roof. The defence is not knowing more verses. It is knowing what they are for.

And the last offer is not a bluff. The kingdoms of the world genuinely are on the table, and they genuinely will be His; Revelation says so. What is being offered is the destination without the road. All of it, now, for one act of worship, and no cross.
"Get behind me, Satan." Those words are worth keeping in reach, because He says them again in chapter 16, to Peter, who has just suggested the same thing in friendlier language.

Then the chapter turns and the ministry starts, and the location matters. Capernaum, in Zebulun and Naphtali. Those were the first tribes Assyria deported, seven centuries of being the forgotten end of the country. Isaiah had promised that the people who sat in darkness would see a great light, and Matthew reports that the light came on in the darkest corner rather than in Jerusalem.
Verse 20 is the last thing to hold. They immediately left their nets. Verse 22 goes further: they left the boat and their father in it. Nobody in that story asks what the terms are.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 5 - The Beatitudes, and "But I Tell You"
chapters.title: The Beatitudes, and "But I Tell You"
keyNotes: He goes up the mountain and sits down. Sitting was the posture of authority for a teacher - and a mountain, with a lawgiver on it, is not an accidental setting (Matthew 5:1).
Nine sentences beginning "blessed." Makarios is not a wish or a hope; it is a declaration that something is already the case, whatever it looks like (Matthew 5:3-12).
"Poor in spirit" uses ptochos, the word for a beggar crouching, not for modest means. It describes someone with nothing to bring (Matthew 5:3).
The first and last beatitudes both say "theirs is the Kingdom" in the present tense, and the seven between them are future. The set is bracketed by something already true (Matthew 5:3, 10).
"The gentle shall inherit the earth" quotes Psalm 37 exactly, a psalm about not fretting over people who are getting away with it (Matthew 5:5).
Salt and light are both useless in storage. Salt cut with impurities, as Galilean salt was, could leach until only the residue was left - flavourless but still looking like salt (Matthew 5:13).
"A city located on a hill can't be hidden" is not a command. It is a fact about what a community of these people is (Matthew 5:14).
Verse 17 governs everything that follows: I did not come to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfill (Matthew 5:17).
Not one yod - the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet - nor one tiny stroke will pass from the law until all is accomplished (Matthew 5:18).
And verse 19 makes teaching others to relax a commandment its own category of offence (Matthew 5:19).

"Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees" cannot mean keeping more rules than the most rule-keeping people alive. It has to mean a different kind of righteousness (Matthew 5:20).
Six times He says "you have heard that it was said... but I tell you." He is not correcting Torah; He is going underneath the act to the wanting that produces it (Matthew 5:21-48).
Murder reaches back to anger and contempt. Raca is Aramaic for something like empty-head, and the sentence for it is the council (Matthew 5:21-22).
Reconciliation outranks worship. Leave the gift at the altar - in Jerusalem, after days of travel - and go and sort it out first (Matthew 5:23-24).
Adultery reaches back to the look that is cultivating it, and the remedy is put in shocking terms about eye and hand (Matthew 5:27-30).
The oath section dismantles a system of graded swearing that existed to create escape hatches. Let your yes be yes (Matthew 5:33-37).
"An eye for an eye" was always a limit on vengeance rather than a licence for it, and He presses past the limit to no retaliation at all (Matthew 5:38-39).
"Love your neighbour and hate your enemy" - the second half of that quotation is not in the Torah anywhere. He is quoting the tradition, not the text (Matthew 5:43).
The chapter lands on teleios, usually rendered perfect - complete, finished, mature - and behind it stands Leviticus: you shall be holy, for I am holy (Matthew 5:48).

intro: He goes up a mountain and sits down to teach, and the staging is doing work before He says anything. A mountain, a teacher, and the law; anyone raised on Exodus knows the shape of that. But there is a difference. Moses went up and God spoke from the fire. Here the one on the mountain opens his own mouth.

The Beatitudes are usually read as gentle. They are not. They are a list of the people the world has already written off, and He calls them blessed, not "will be one day if they hang on," but blessed now, as a statement of fact. The beggared, the grieving, the ones with no leverage, the ones hungry for a rightness they cannot produce. The qualification for that list is having nothing to bring.

Then salt and light, and both images have the same point. Salt kept in the jar and a lamp put under a basket are not merely wasted; they have stopped being what they are for. And a city on a hill is not being commanded to be visible. It simply is. Visibility is not the goal. It is the by-product of actually being different.

Now verse 17, which governs everything else in this sermon and is worth reading slowly. "Don't think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn't come to destroy, but to fulfill." And then the strongest possible reinforcement: not one yod, the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet, not one stroke of a pen, until all is accomplished. Whatever is happening in the six paragraphs that follow, it is not abolition.

Because what happens next sounds like abolition if it is read carelessly. Six times: you have heard that it was said, but I tell you. Look at what actually changes. The commandment against murder stays; He adds that the anger underneath it is already the same country. The commandment against adultery stays; He adds that the look cultivating it has already arrived. He is not loosening anything. He is going down to the root and saying the root is the thing.

That is what verse 20 means. A righteousness exceeding the scribes and Pharisees cannot mean keeping more rules than the most fastidious rule-keepers in the country; that is a race nobody wins. It has to mean a different kind of righteousness altogether, one that starts inside, where no one is watching, which is exactly where the next chapter goes.

One correction is worth having. In verse 43 He quotes "love your neighbour and hate your enemy," and the second half of that is nowhere in the Torah. Leviticus says love your neighbour; nothing says hate your enemy. He is quoting what people had made of the text, not the text itself, which is its own quiet lesson about how traditions grow.

The last verse deserves honesty. Be perfect, as your Father is perfect. The word is teleios: complete, brought to its intended end, mature. It is not a demand for flawlessness so much as a call to be finished rather than half-made. Which is still, on any honest accounting, well past anything a person can do alone.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 6 - In Secret, and the Eye That Fills the Body
chapters.title: In Secret, and the Eye That Fills the Body
keyNotes: Three acts of devotion - giving, praying, fasting - each handled in the same three moves: don't perform it, do it unseen, and your Father who sees in secret will repay (Matthew 6:1-18).
Hypokrites is a theatre word. It meant an actor, someone speaking from behind a mask (Matthew 6:2).
"They have received their reward" translates apecho, the term written on a receipt: paid in full, account closed. They got exactly what they were buying (Matthew 6:2).
The trumpet in verse 2 is almost certainly figurative; what is literal is the instinct to make sure generosity is noticed (Matthew 6:2).
"Don't let your left hand know what your right hand does" is deliberately impossible, which is the point - give without auditing your own generosity (Matthew 6:3).
The inner room is the tameion, the storeroom - in a peasant house, the one room with a door that shuts (Matthew 6:6).
"Vain repetitions" is battalogeo, something like babbling. The problem is not length; it is the idea that volume of words moves God (Matthew 6:7).
"Your Father knows what things you need before you ask him" removes informing God as the reason to pray, which leaves relationship as the reason (Matthew 6:8).
The prayer has six petitions. The first three are about Him - name, kingdom, will - and only then do we get to bread (Matthew 6:9-13).
It begins "our Father," in the plural, in a prayer prayed behind a shut door (Matthew 6:6, 9).
"Daily" is epiousios, a word that barely exists elsewhere in Greek. It may mean for the coming day, or simply sufficient (Matthew 6:11).
Debts, not faults. Opheilema is the commercial word for what is owed (Matthew 6:12).
Forgiveness is the one petition He returns to and expands after the prayer ends (Matthew 6:14-15).
Fasting is to be invisible: anoint your head and wash your face, which is to say, look like an ordinary Tuesday (Matthew 6:16-18).
Moth, corrosion and burglars are all named for the same reason - everything stored on earth is being quietly eaten from somewhere (Matthew 6:19).
Verse 21 runs the opposite way to expectation. Not where your heart is your treasure goes, but where your treasure is your heart follows. You can move the heart by moving the money (Matthew 6:21).
The lamp of the body is the eye, and the words rendered sound and evil are Hebrew idiom for generous and stingy. In context this whole paragraph is still about money (Matthew 6:22-23).
No one can serve two masters - a slave could not have two owners. Mammon is simply Aramaic for wealth (Matthew 6:24).
The argument against anxiety is from lesser to greater: birds are fed, grass that will be fuel by tomorrow is dressed better than Solomon (Matthew 6:26-30).
"Which of you by being anxious can add one cubit to his lifespan" - worry is not merely wrong, it is ineffective (Matthew 6:27).
Verse 33 is where the chapter has been going all along: seek first the Kingdom, and the rest is added (Matthew 6:33).
And it ends almost dryly: each day's own evil is sufficient. There is enough today (Matthew 6:34).

intro: Chapter 5 went underneath the commandments to the wanting. Chapter 6 goes underneath the religion to the audience.

Three times He takes something genuinely good, giving, praying, fasting, and asks the same question of each: who is watching, and is that why you are doing it? The word He uses for the people who get this wrong is hypokrites, which was not originally an insult. It was the word for an actor, someone delivering lines from behind a mask.

And His verdict on them is not that they get nothing. It is that they get paid. "They have received their reward" is apecho, the phrase written across the bottom of a bill: settled in full. They wanted to be seen, they were seen, the transaction is closed. There is nothing outstanding.

Then the prayer, and the first thing to notice is its order. Six petitions, and the first three have nothing to do with us: your name, your kingdom, your will. Only after that does it reach bread. Most praying starts at verse 11 and works backwards, if it gets there at all.

The second thing to notice is that this prayer is plural. Our Father. Give us. Forgive us. And He has just said to pray it behind a shut door, alone. Even in the storeroom no one prays as an only child.

And He returns to exactly one petition after the prayer finishes. Not the bread, not the kingdom, the forgiveness. Verses 14 and 15 are a hard pair, and they do not say that forgiving earns forgiveness. They say that a hand clenched shut cannot receive anything, including this.

Then the chapter turns to money, and it never really turns away again. Treasure, the eye, two masters, anxiety, all of it is one argument. Verse 21 is the hinge, and it runs backwards from what most people expect. We assume treasure follows the heart, and so we wait to feel generous. He says the heart follows the treasure. Move the money and the affections come along behind it, which is either alarming or the most practical thing in the sermon.

The line about the eye is easy to misread as being about focus. In Hebrew idiom a good eye means a generous person and an evil eye means a tight-fisted one; Proverbs uses it that way. Read like that, the passage has not changed subject at all. It is still about money, sitting between treasure and mammon exactly where it belongs.

Verse 34 is almost funny after everything else. Do not be anxious about tomorrow. Each day's own evil is sufficient. There is enough today. He is not promising an easy life; He is saying that borrowing tomorrow's trouble adds to a pile that was already full without it.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 7 - The Beam, the Narrow Gate, and Two Houses in the Same Storm
chapters.title: The Beam, the Narrow Gate, and Two Houses in the Same Storm
keyNotes: "Don't judge" is the most quoted and least finished sentence in the sermon. Verse 5 ends with "then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother's eye" - which assumes the speck still comes out (Matthew 7:1-5).
The standard is reciprocal: with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you (Matthew 7:2).
The image is deliberately absurd, and it comes out of a carpenter's mouth - a sawdust splinter in one eye and a load-bearing beam in the other (Matthew 7:3-4).

Verse 6 sits immediately beside the ban on judging and requires exactly the discernment verse 1 seemed to forbid. The two are not in conflict; condemning and discerning are different acts (Matthew 7:6).
Ask, seek, knock are continuous imperatives - keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking (Matthew 7:7).
The bread and the stone, the fish and the serpent, are pairs that look alike. A father is not in the business of handing over convincing counterfeits (Matthew 7:9-10).
"If you then, being evil" is dropped in without argument, as a premise nobody in the crowd is expected to dispute (Matthew 7:11).
The Golden Rule here is positive rather than negative - not merely refrain from harm, but do the good you would want done - and He says it sums up the law and the prophets (Matthew 7:12).
Two gates, two roads, two crowds, two destinations. The wide one is described first and is described as crowded (Matthew 7:13-14).
False prophets come in sheep's clothing, which is the whole difficulty: they are dressed as the flock, not as wolves (Matthew 7:15).
The test offered is fruit - not gifting, not crowd size, not results (Matthew 7:16-20).
Verses 21 to 23 are the most frightening paragraph in the sermon. Prophecy, exorcism and mighty works, all done in His name, and the verdict is still no (Matthew 7:21-22).
"I never knew you" is not the language of something lost. It is the language of something that was never there (Matthew 7:23).
The two houses face identical weather. Same rain, same floods, same wind. The difference is the foundation, which is the one thing nobody can see until the storm (Matthew 7:24-27).
And the foundation is defined precisely: hearing these words and doing them. Hearing alone puts you in the second house (Matthew 7:24, 26).
The crowd's reaction is about authority. The scribes taught by citing which rabbi said what; He simply said it (Matthew 7:28-29).

intro: Verse 1 is the most quoted sentence in the sermon and almost nobody finishes the paragraph. Read to verse 5 and the instruction is not "never assess anything." It is: deal with your own eye first, and then, in His words, you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother's eye. The speck still comes out. What changes is who is qualified to be holding the tweezers.
And the picture is a carpenter's joke. A speck of sawdust in one eye, and a roof beam in the other. He grew up in a workshop; those are both things He would have swept off a floor.

Then verse 6, which sits jarringly close to verse 1. Do not give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls to pigs, which requires working out who is which. So within six verses the reader is told not to condemn and required to discern, and if that feels contradictory it is worth noticing that they are different acts. One is a verdict on a person. The other is wisdom about what to do next.

The middle of the chapter is warm, ask, seek, knock, a Father who gives good things, and then it narrows. Two gates. Two roads. And the honest detail is that the wide one is described as crowded and the narrow one as found by few. He does not soften that.

The false prophets come in sheep's clothing, and that is the entire problem. Nobody is fooled by a wolf. The test He gives is not doctrine, or gifting, or how many follow them. It is fruit, what actually grows out of a life over time, which is slower and less exciting than any other test and is the only one He offers.

Which sets up verses 21 to 23, and these should frighten anyone who has ever been impressed by results. Prophecy. Exorcism. Mighty works. All in His name, all apparently real, and the answer is "I never knew you." Not "you fell away." Never. It is possible to do remarkable things in the name of someone you do not actually know.

And then the two houses. Notice what is identical: the rain, the floods, the wind. Both men get the same storm. Notice what is also probably identical: how the houses looked on a clear day. The only difference is underneath, where nobody can see it, and it does not matter at all until the weather comes.

His definition of the foundation is worth holding plainly. Not everyone who hears these words: everyone who hears these words and does them. The sermon ends by saying that hearing it is not the point of it.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 8 - A Leper Touched, a Centurion's Faith, and a Boat Filling With Water
chapters.title: A Leper Touched, a Centurion's Faith, and a Boat Filling With Water
keyNotes: Matthew has given us the King's words; now he gives us the King's works. Chapters 8 and 9 are a deliberate block of demonstrations (Matthew 8:1).
The leper's question is not whether Yahshua can, but whether He wants to. That is the harder doubt (Matthew 8:2).
He touches him. Under Leviticus, contact with a leper made a person unclean - and here the traffic runs the other way (Matthew 8:3).
"I want to" answers the actual question before "be made clean" answers the situation (Matthew 8:3).
He then sends the man to the priest with the offering Moses commanded. The Torah procedure is kept, not bypassed (Matthew 8:4).
The centurion is a Gentile and an officer of an occupying army - about the least likely person in Galilee to be commended (Matthew 8:5).
His reasoning is military. He knows how delegated authority works, and he recognises that sickness takes orders from Yahshua the way soldiers take orders from him (Matthew 8:8-9).
Yahshua marvels, which the Gospels record Him doing only twice - here at a Gentile's faith, and later at his own town's unbelief (Matthew 8:10).
Verses 11 and 12 are startling in the most Jewish of the Gospels: many from east and west at the table with Abraham, and the children of the Kingdom outside (Matthew 8:11-12).
Peter has a mother-in-law, which means Peter has a wife - something Paul mentions in passing years later (Matthew 8:14).
She gets up and serves them. Healing in this Gospel usually restores someone to a function, not just to health (Matthew 8:15).
Verse 17 applies Isaiah 53 - the Servant who took our infirmities - to a night of healing rather than to the cross (Matthew 8:17).
Two would-be followers: a scribe who volunteers enthusiastically and a disciple who asks for a delay. Both get answers that sound harsh (Matthew 8:19-22).
"The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head" is the reply to the volunteer. The cost is stated before the commitment, not after (Matthew 8:20).
"Let the dead bury their own dead" almost certainly concerns the second burial - a rite performed about a year after death - so the request is for a year's postponement (Matthew 8:21-22).
The word for the storm is seismos, the word for an earthquake. And He is asleep in it (Matthew 8:24).
He addresses the fear before He addresses the weather: why are you fearful, and only then does He rebuke the wind (Matthew 8:26).
"What kind of man is this?" is the right question, and Psalm 107 has already answered it - it is Yahweh who stills the storm (Matthew 8:27).
The far shore is Gentile country, which is why there is a herd of pigs in it (Matthew 8:28-30).
The demons ask not to be tormented "before the time," which means they know there is a timetable and that they are on it (Matthew 8:29).
The town's response to a man restored is to ask Him to leave. The pigs mattered more (Matthew 8:34).

intro: Chapters 8 and 9 are a deliberate block. Matthew has given the King's words; now he gives the King's works, and the first thing that happens is a man nobody would touch.
Notice what the leper actually asks. Not whether Yahshua can, but whether He wants to. That is the harder doubt, and it is the one most people are actually carrying.

And then the touch, which under Leviticus should have made Yahshua unclean. The traffic runs the other way. He answers the question that was asked before He answers the situation: I want to, and then, be made clean. And He sends the man to the priest with the offering Moses commanded, so the Torah procedure is kept rather than bypassed.

The centurion is the least likely person in Galilee to be commended, being both a Gentile and an officer of an occupying army. And his reasoning is entirely military. He understands delegated authority from the inside, and he works out that sickness takes orders from Yahshua the way soldiers take orders from him. Yahshua marvels, which the Gospels record Him doing exactly twice: here at a Gentile's faith, and later at His own town's unbelief.
Verses 11 and 12 are startling in the most Jewish of the Gospels. Many from east and west at the table with Abraham, and the children of the Kingdom outside.
Then Peter's mother-in-law, which incidentally tells us Peter has a wife, and she gets up and serves them. Healing in this Gospel usually restores someone to a function, not merely to health.

The two would-be followers get answers that sound harsh. To the enthusiastic volunteer: the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. The cost is stated before the commitment, not after. To the man asking to bury his father: let the dead bury their own dead. That request almost certainly concerns the second burial, a rite performed about a year after death, which makes it a request for a year's delay rather than an afternoon's.

Then the boat, and the word Matthew uses for the storm is seismos, the word for an earthquake. And He is asleep in it. When they wake Him He addresses the fear before He addresses the weather: why are you fearful, and only then does He speak to the wind.

The chapter ends with a town that watched a man be freed from a legion of demons and asked Yahshua to leave, because of the pigs. That is the last picture: a place that preferred its economy to its deliverer.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 9 - Authority to Forgive, a Tax Booth, and Sheep Without a Shepherd
chapters.title: Authority to Forgive, a Tax Booth, and Sheep Without a Shepherd
keyNotes: It is the friends' faith that Matthew records - Jesus, seeing their faith - not the paralytic's (Matthew 9:2).
And He addresses the sins before the paralysis. Nobody in the room came for that (Matthew 9:2).
The scribes are right about the principle: only God forgives sins. Their premise is sound and their conclusion is the error (Matthew 9:3).
"Which is easier to say?" is a sharp question. Saying either is equally easy; doing the visible one is what testifies to the invisible one (Matthew 9:5-6).
"Son of Man" is not a modest self-description. It is the title of the figure in Daniel 7 who receives everlasting dominion (Matthew 9:6).
Matthew names himself by his trade in his own Gospel. Mark and Luke, telling the same story, call him Levi (Matthew 9:9).
Tax collectors were contractors for Rome, taking a cut on top - collaborators as well as profiteers (Matthew 9:9).
Two words and he goes. Fishermen could return to their nets; a man who walked away from a tax franchise was not getting it back (Matthew 9:9).
The offence is the meal, not the conversation. Eating with someone meant accepting them (Matthew 9:10-11).
"Go and learn what this means" was a standard rabbinic rebuke to a teacher who ought to know better - roughly, go do your homework (Matthew 9:13).
What He sends them to learn is Hosea 6:6: I desire mercy and not sacrifice (Matthew 9:13).
The fasting question gets a wedding for an answer, and the first quiet hint that the bridegroom will be taken away (Matthew 9:15).
The new cloth and new wineskins are not a dismissal of what is old. They are about what can hold what is coming (Matthew 9:16-17).
Two stories are interleaved, and both turn on twelve - a woman bleeding twelve years, and a girl who has lived twelve (Matthew 9:18-25).
Both are situations of ritual uncleanness - a haemorrhage and a corpse - and in both the cleanness travels outward instead of the uncleanness travelling in (Matthew 9:20-25).
She reaches for the fringe of His garment, the tzitzit that Numbers commands. The Hebrew for corner and for wing is the same word, and Malachi promised healing in his wings (Matthew 9:20).
"The girl isn't dead, but sleeping" gets Him laughed at by professional mourners who knew death when they saw it (Matthew 9:24).
Two blind men call Him son of David - the first time anyone in this Gospel uses a messianic title to His face (Matthew 9:27).
The Pharisees' explanation of the exorcism is the prince of demons, which is the first appearance of an accusation that will grow (Matthew 9:34).
Verse 35 repeats chapter 4 word for word, closing the bracket around the words and the works (Matthew 9:35).
"Moved with compassion" is splanchnizomai - felt in the gut, not decided in the head (Matthew 9:36).
"Harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd" is Moses' phrase and Ezekiel's indictment, now spoken looking at a crowd (Matthew 9:36).
The command is to pray for labourers - and the very next chapter sends the men who prayed it (Matthew 9:37-38).

intro: Four men carry a friend to a house so crowded they cannot get in, and Matthew says Yahshua saw their faith. Not the paralytic's. Theirs. Somebody else's faith is doing the carrying in this story, which is worth saying out loud to anyone who feels they have run out of their own.

And then He treats the deeper problem first. The man came for his legs and is told his sins are forgiven, which is not what anyone in the room was expecting, including the man on the mat. The healing follows as evidence rather than as the point.
The scribes are right about the theology. Only God forgives sins; saying so about yourself is blasphemy. They have the syllogism correct and only one premise wrong.

Then Matthew's own call, told in half a verse. He is sitting at a tax booth, which in that world meant he had bought the right to collect for Rome and made his living on the margin. And that is a job you cannot go back to. Fishermen could return to their nets, and in fact do. A tax collector who walks away from a booth has burned it.

So the dinner that follows is the natural thing: he throws a party and fills the house with the only friends he has, which is to say the people no respectable person would eat with. And the Pharisees ask the disciples rather than Yahshua, which is its own small cowardice.

His answer quotes Hosea and adds a homework assignment: go and learn what this means, I desire mercy and not sacrifice. That phrase comes back in chapter 12, in a fight about the Sabbath. It is His standing answer to religion without compassion.

Then the questions about fasting, and the images He reaches for are both about strain. New cloth on an old garment tears it. New wine in old skins bursts them. He is not saying the old is bad. He is saying that what He has brought will not fit inside the existing arrangements, and forcing it will damage both.

And then two stories folded into one another: a ruler whose daughter has just died, and a woman on the road who has been bleeding for twelve years. Twelve years of uncleanness, meaning twelve years of not being touched. She reaches for the fringe of His garment, which was the part carrying the commanded tassels, and Yahshua stops a dying girl's rescue to speak to her and call her daughter.

The chapter closes with the sentence the next chapter grows out of. He saw the crowds and was moved with compassion, and the Greek is a gut word, and He said the harvest is plentiful but the labourers are few. Pray for labourers. And in chapter 10 the men who prayed it get sent.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 10 - Twelve Names, Sheep Among Wolves, and a Sparrow That Falls
chapters.title: Twelve Names, Sheep Among Wolves, and a Sparrow That Falls
keyNotes: Chapter 9 ended with a prayer for labourers; chapter 10 opens with the men who prayed it being sent. He does not send in answer to the prayer so much as He sends the people praying (Matthew 9:38, 10:1).
Authority is given before instruction is given. They are equipped first and briefed second (Matthew 10:1).
The list of twelve names includes "Matthew the tax collector" - the author labelling himself with the job he was called out of, which nobody else in the lists does (Matthew 10:3).
It also ends with Judas, named as betrayer at the moment of commissioning. He is sent out with real authority anyway (Matthew 10:4).

The first mission is restricted: not to Gentiles, not to Samaritans, but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. The restriction is a stage, not a policy - by chapter 28 it is all nations (Matthew 10:5-6).
"Freely you received, so freely give" is the fee schedule. What was not bought cannot be sold (Matthew 10:8).
They travel with nothing - no money, no bag, no spare coat - which makes them dependent on the hospitality of the towns they are sent to (Matthew 10:9-10).
Shaking the dust off the feet was what a Jew did on leaving Gentile soil. Used on a Jewish town that refuses the message, it is a deliberate insult and a formal verdict (Matthew 10:14).
"Sheep among wolves" is not encouragement. He tells them the odds before they go (Matthew 10:16).
Wise as serpents and harmless as doves holds two things together that most people separate - shrewdness without malice, innocence without naivety (Matthew 10:16).
The promise about what to say in that hour is given specifically for trials, not for sermon preparation (Matthew 10:19-20).
The family language is brutal and He does not soften it: brother delivering brother, children against parents (Matthew 10:21).
"He who endures to the end will be saved" is set inside persecution, not inside doctrine (Matthew 10:22).
"If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul" - He is warning them two chapters before it actually happens in 12:24 (Matthew 10:25).
Fear is addressed three times in five verses, and each time the cure is a fact about the Father rather than a feeling to work up (Matthew 10:26-31).
An assarion was worth about an hour of a labourer's wage, and bought two sparrows. Not one of them falls without the Father (Matthew 10:29).
"I came not to send peace, but a sword" is aimed at households, and the wording in verse 35 is lifted almost intact out of Micah (Matthew 10:34-36).
The first mention of the cross in this Gospel comes long before Golgotha, and it is addressed to followers rather than to Him (Matthew 10:38).
The chapter ends small: a cup of cold water. After sword and cross and courts, the last instruction is about a drink of water (Matthew 10:42).

intro: Notice where this chapter begins. Chapter 9 closed with Yahshua looking at the crowds, moved in the gut, telling His disciples to pray that the Lord of the harvest would send out labourers. Then chapter 10 opens and He sends them. They prayed for workers and became the answer to their own prayer. That happens more often than anyone would like.

Then the list of names, and two of them are worth stopping on. Matthew calls himself "Matthew the tax collector," and his is the only list that does. Mark and Luke leave the job off. He keeps it on, years later, in his own book. And the list ends with Judas, identified as the betrayer at the moment he is being handed authority to cast out demons. Whatever Judas did later, what he received here was real.

The instructions are strange on first reading. No money. No bag. No spare coat. He is deliberately making them dependent on the hospitality of the very towns they are being sent to, which means the mission cannot be done at arm's length. And where a town will not receive them, they shake the dust off their feet, which is what a Jew did coming home off Gentile soil. Done on a Jewish street, that gesture says something very sharp.

Then the tone shifts. Sheep among wolves. Councils. Floggings in synagogues. Governors and kings. Brother handing over brother. He tells them all of this before they go, not after. He has never been in the business of recruiting people who did not know what they were signing up for.

And in the middle of it, three times, He says do not be afraid, and the cure He gives is never a feeling. It is always a fact about the Father. Nothing hidden stays hidden. The one who can destroy soul and body is the one worth fearing. And two sparrows cost about an hour's wage, and not one of them falls without Him. He does not say the sparrow does not fall. He says it does not fall unnoticed.

The hardest verses are near the end. Not peace but a sword. A man's foes will be those of his own household, and that line is lifted almost word for word out of Micah 7. He is not predicting a war between nations. He is saying the dinner table is where this will cost the most.
And the chapter ends small. After swords and crosses and courts, the last instruction is a cup of cold water given to a little one. The scale drops right down. It usually does.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 11 - A Question from Prison, Woe to the Cities, and an Easy Yoke
chapters.title: A Question from Prison, Woe to the Cities, and an Easy Yoke
keyNotes: John the Baptizer, who saw the heavens open and heard the voice at the Jordan, sends from prison to ask whether Yahshua is the one. Certainty and doubt can live in the same man (Matthew 11:2-3).
Yahshua does not rebuke the question. He answers it with evidence - go and tell John what you hear and see (Matthew 11:4).
The list He sends back is a stitched quotation from Isaiah: blind, lame, lepers, deaf, dead, poor. It is a claim made in Isaiah's own vocabulary (Matthew 11:5).

The one thing conspicuously absent from that list is prisoners set free - which was the part John most needed. He answers the question John asked, not the one he was living in (Matthew 11:5, Isaiah 61:1).
"Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me" is spoken to a man in a cell. It is tender and it is honest at the same time (Matthew 11:6).
Having answered John's doubt privately, He defends John publicly. The crowd hears no hint that John wavered (Matthew 11:7-11).
"A reed shaken by the wind" is exactly what a wavering man looks like - and He says that is precisely what John is not (Matthew 11:7).
The greatest born of women is still less than the least in the Kingdom. Position in the Kingdom is not a reward for stature (Matthew 11:11).
"This is Elijah, who is to come" is qualified: if you are willing to receive it. The fulfilment is offered rather than forced (Matthew 11:14).

The generation is compared to children who will play neither wedding nor funeral. John fasted and was called demonised; Yahshua ate and was called a glutton. The objection was never really about the diet (Matthew 11:16-19).
The woes fall on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum - the towns that saw the most. Judgment is measured against light received (Matthew 11:20-24).
Capernaum was His own base of operations, and it gets the sharpest word of the three (Matthew 11:23).
The prayer in verse 25 thanks the Father for hiding things from the wise and revealing them to infants - which is not anti-intellectual so much as anti-self-sufficient (Matthew 11:25).
Verse 27 is the most John-like sentence in Matthew: all things delivered to the Son, and mutual knowing between Father and Son (Matthew 11:27).
The invitation is to the labouring and heavily burdened - which in context includes those crushed under religious requirement (Matthew 11:28).
A yoke is for work, and it is built for two. He does not offer the removal of the yoke; He offers His (Matthew 11:29-30).
"Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart" is the only place in the Gospels He describes His own character directly (Matthew 11:29).

intro: Start with who is asking the question. This is John. The man who saw the sky open at the Jordan and heard the voice. The man who said behold the Lamb of God. And now he is in Herod's prison sending word out to ask: are you the one, or should we look for somebody else. Anyone who has ever been sure of something and then found themselves asking anyway is in good company.

Watch what Yahshua does not do. He does not scold him. He does not question his faith. He sends back a list, blind see, lame walk, lepers cleansed, deaf hear, dead raised, poor evangelised, and the list is stitched together out of Isaiah. It is an answer in the language John had spent his life reading.

But there is a gap in it, and it is worth being honest about. Isaiah 61 says the Spirit is on Him to proclaim liberty to the captives and the opening of the prison to those who are bound. That phrase does not come back in the reply. The prison door does not open. John is beheaded in the next chapter. So the sentence that follows, blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me, is spoken directly into a life that is not going to be rescued.

Then, the moment John's messengers are out of earshot, Yahshua defends him. A reed shaken by the wind is precisely what a wavering man looks like, and He tells the crowd that is exactly what John is not. He handles the doubt in private and the reputation in public. That order is worth learning.

The middle of the chapter turns hard. A generation that would play neither wedding nor funeral: John fasted and they said he had a demon, Yahshua ate and they called Him a drunkard. When people have decided in advance, the reason they give is never the real reason. And then woe to Chorazin, woe to Bethsaida, woe to Capernaum, which was His own town and gets the worst of it. The measure is not how bad a place is. It is how much it saw.

And then, with no transition at all, comes the sentence people put on walls. Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. It arrives straight after the woes, and what He offers is not the removal of a yoke but His yoke. A yoke is for working, and it is built for two.
Verse 29 is the one place in the Gospels He describes His own character outright. Gentle and humble in heart. That is who is doing the inviting.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 12 - A Bruised Reed, an Unforgivable Word, and the Sign of Jonah
chapters.title: A Bruised Reed, an Unforgivable Word, and the Sign of Jonah
keyNotes: The disciples are not accused of theft. Torah expressly permits plucking a neighbour's grain by hand. The charge is that they did it on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:1-2).
His first defence is not from law but from narrative - David ate the show bread, which was flatly unlawful for him, and Scripture does not condemn him (Matthew 12:3-4).
His second defence is sharper: the priests break the Sabbath every Sabbath by working in the temple, and are guiltless. The temple overrides the day (Matthew 12:5).
Then the claim under both: one greater than the temple is here. If the temple can justify Sabbath work, so can He (Matthew 12:6).
He quotes Hosea again - I desire mercy, and not sacrifice - the same verse He used at Matthew's table in chapter 9. It is His standing answer to religion without compassion (Matthew 12:7).
"Lord of the Sabbath" is a claim about the day, not an abolition of it. A Lord of something does not thereby cancel it (Matthew 12:8).
The question about the withered hand is asked "that they might accuse him" - the man is being used as bait (Matthew 12:10).
His counter-question is practical and unanswerable: you would pull your own sheep out of a pit on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:11-12).
The conspiracy to destroy Him begins here, in chapter 12, over a healed hand (Matthew 12:14).
Knowing they mean to kill Him, He withdraws and keeps healing, and tells people not to publicise it. Matthew reads this as Isaiah's servant who will not shout in the streets (Matthew 12:15-19).
"He won't break a bruised reed. He won't quench a smoking flax" - a reed already crushed and a wick already guttering. Both are things anyone else would throw out (Matthew 12:20).
The Beelzebul charge is a concession before it is an attack: they do not deny the exorcism, only its source (Matthew 12:24).
The house-divided argument turns it back on them - and then the counter-question, by whom do your own people cast them out (Matthew 12:26-27).
The strong man must be bound before the house is plundered. The exorcisms are not skirmishes; they are looting a house already secured (Matthew 12:29).
The unforgivable word is spoken in this specific context: watching the Spirit work and calling it demonic. It is not a slip of the tongue but a settled verdict (Matthew 12:31-32).
Words are treated as evidence rather than as offence - out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, so speech is the readout, not the disease (Matthew 12:34-37).
They ask for a sign immediately after being given one. The sign refused is replaced by the sign of Jonah - three days and three nights (Matthew 12:38-40).
Nineveh and the queen of the south will stand up in judgment against this generation. Both were Gentiles who responded to less (Matthew 12:41-42).
The swept and empty house is a warning about reformation without occupation. Cleaned out is not the same as filled (Matthew 12:43-45).
The chapter ends with family redefined - whoever does the will of my Father is my brother, sister and mother - while His own mother and brothers wait outside (Matthew 12:46-50).

intro: Two Sabbath scenes open this chapter, and it is worth being precise about what is actually being argued. Nobody accuses the disciples of stealing. Deuteronomy expressly allows plucking a neighbour's grain by hand. The complaint is the day.

And His answers are not what a reader expects. The first is a story, not a statute: David ate the show bread, which was unambiguously not lawful for him, and Scripture never condemns him for it. The second is closer to the bone: the priests work every Sabbath in the temple and are guiltless, because the temple outranks the day. Then He lands it. One greater than the temple is here.

The second scene is uglier. There is a man with a withered hand, and the question about healing is asked, Matthew tells us plainly, so that they might accuse Him. The man is bait. And it is over that healed hand, in verse 14, that they first conspire to destroy Him.

Which is exactly where Matthew puts the longest Old Testament quotation in his Gospel. Knowing they mean to kill Him, Yahshua withdraws, keeps healing, and tells people to keep quiet, and Matthew says: this is Isaiah's servant. He will not strive or shout. He will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoking flax. Consider what those two things are. A reed already crushed, useless as a pipe. A wick already guttering, more smoke than light. Anyone else throws both out.

Then the accusation that He casts out demons by Beelzebul, and notice that they concede the exorcism. They cannot deny what happened, only relabel it. His reply is logic first, a kingdom divided cannot stand, and then a question they cannot answer: by whom do your own people cast them out?

Which brings the reader to the paragraph that has frightened more sincere believers than almost any other. The word against the Spirit that will not be forgiven. Keep it in its context. These are men watching the Spirit of God set someone free and calling it the work of hell, and not in a moment of anger, but as a settled position they have decided to hold. Someone anxious about whether they have committed it has, by that very anxiety, given the strongest evidence they have not.

And then a demand for a sign, right after a sign. He gives them Jonah, three days and three nights, and then two Gentile examples, Nineveh and the queen of the south, who responded to far less than this generation has been handed.

The last picture is the one to hold. A house swept clean and left empty is worse off than before, because empty does not stay empty. And then the door opens and His mother and brothers are outside, and He redefines family around doing the will of the Father. This is a chapter about who really belongs to Him.

verses.1: At that time, Jesus went on the Sabbath day through the grain fields. His disciples were hungry and began to pluck heads of grain and to eat.
verses.2: But the Pharisees, when they saw it, said to him, “Behold, your disciples do what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.”
verses.3: But he said to them, “Haven’t you read what David did, when he was hungry, and those who were with him;
verses.4: how he entered into God’s house, and ate the show bread, which was not lawful for him to eat, neither for those who were with him, but only for the priests?
verses.5: Or have you not read in the law, that on the Sabbath day, the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath, and are guiltless?
verses.6: But I tell you that one greater than the temple is here.
verses.7: But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you wouldn’t have condemned the guiltless.
verses.8: For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
verses.9: He departed there, and went into their synagogue.
verses.10: And behold there was a man with a withered hand. They asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath day?” that they might accuse him.
verses.11: He said to them, “What man is there among you, who has one sheep, and if this one falls into a pit on the Sabbath day, won’t he grab on to it, and lift it out?
verses.12: Of how much more value then is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath day.”
verses.13: Then he told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out; and it was restored whole, just like the other.
verses.14: But the Pharisees went out, and conspired against him, how they might destroy him.
verses.15: Jesus, perceiving that, withdrew from there. Great multitudes followed him; and he healed them all,
verses.16: and commanded them that they should not make him known:
verses.17: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying,
verses.18: “Behold, my servant whom I have chosen; my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my Spirit on him. He will proclaim justice to the nations.
verses.19: He will not strive, nor shout; neither will anyone hear his voice in the streets.
verses.20: He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax, until he leads justice to victory.
verses.21: In his name, the nations will hope.”
verses.22: Then one possessed by a demon, blind and mute, was brought to him and he healed him, so that the blind and mute man both spoke and saw.
verses.23: All the multitudes were amazed, and said, “Can this be the son of David?”
verses.24: But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “This man does not cast out demons, except by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons.”
verses.25: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand.
verses.26: If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand?
verses.27: If I by Beelzebul cast out demons, by whom do your children cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verses.28: But if I by the Spirit of God cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come upon you.
verses.29: Or how can one enter into the house of the strong man, and plunder his goods, unless he first bind the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.
verses.30: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who doesn’t gather with me, scatters.
verses.31: Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven men.
verses.32: Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age, nor in that which is to come.
verses.33: “Either make the tree good, and its fruit good, or make the tree corrupt, and its fruit corrupt; for the tree is known by its fruit.
verses.34: You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.
verses.35: The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things.
verses.36: I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment.
verses.37: For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”
verses.38: Then certain of the scribes and Pharisees answered, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from you.”
verses.39: But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks after a sign, but no sign will be given to it but the sign of Jonah the prophet.
verses.40: For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
verses.41: The men of Nineveh will stand up in the judgment with this generation, and will condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, someone greater than Jonah is here.
verses.42: The queen of the south will rise up in the judgment with this generation, and will condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, someone greater than Solomon is here.
verses.43: When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it.
verses.44: Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order.
verses.45: Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first. Even so will it be also to this evil generation.”
verses.46: While he was yet speaking to the multitudes, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, seeking to speak to him.
verses.47: One said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside, seeking to speak to you.”
verses.48: But he answered him who spoke to him, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?”
verses.49: He stretched out his hand towards his disciples, and said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers!
verses.50: For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.”
