chapters.heading: CHAPTER 13 - Four Soils, an Enemy Who Sows at Night, and a Pearl Worth Everything
chapters.title: Four Soils, an Enemy Who Sows at Night, and a Pearl Worth Everything
keyNotes: Seven parables in one chapter, four told to the crowd from a boat and three told to the disciples in a house. The venue changes halfway through (Matthew 13:2, 36).
The sower does not sort the ground before he throws. The same seed goes everywhere (Matthew 13:3-8).
Three of the four soils receive the seed and only one of them ends in fruit. That ratio is not softened anywhere in the explanation (Matthew 13:19-23).
The rocky ground is the fastest to sprout. Speed of response is not a measure of depth of root (Matthew 13:5, 20-21).
The thorns do not deny the word; they crowd it. Cares and riches choke rather than argue (Matthew 13:22).
Parables are given as a response to a hardening that has already happened - He quotes Isaiah 6 to explain why He is now speaking this way (Matthew 13:13-15).
"Blessed are your eyes" is said to twelve ordinary men, contrasted with prophets and righteous men who longed to see it and did not (Matthew 13:16-17).
In the wheat and the weeds, the servants' instinct is to pull. The owner's answer is that premature sorting costs wheat (Matthew 13:28-29).
The darnel of that region looks almost exactly like wheat until the heads form. Telling them apart early is not just risky, it is genuinely difficult (Matthew 13:26).
The mustard seed and the yeast are both about something small and hidden that ends up everywhere. One grows visibly, one works invisibly (Matthew 13:31-33).
The treasure is stumbled on and the pearl is searched for. Both men sell everything, and both do it with joy rather than reluctance (Matthew 13:44-46).
The dragnet gathers every kind and the sorting happens at the shore, not in the water - the same pattern as the weeds (Matthew 13:47-50).
The scribe trained for the Kingdom brings out new and old. Neither one replaces the other (Matthew 13:52).
In His own town they get the facts right - carpenter's son, Mary, the brothers by name - and draw exactly the wrong conclusion from them (Matthew 13:55-56).
"He didn't do many mighty works there because of their unbelief" is one of the most sobering sentences in the Gospel (Matthew 13:58).

intro: Notice first that the disciples ask a question most readers skip. Not "what does the parable mean" but "why are you speaking to them this way at all." Something has changed. Chapter 12 ended with men watching the Spirit work and calling it Beelzebul, and now He starts telling stories. His answer quotes Isaiah 6: hearing they do not hear. The parables are not a teaching technique to make things simpler. They come after a hardening, and they sort the people listening.

Then the four soils, and there is a number in there that is easy to hurry past. Three out of four receive the seed. Only one bears fruit. And the sower does not survey the ground first; the same seed goes on the path, the rocks, the thorns and the good earth alike.

Look closely at the rocky ground. It is the fastest. It springs up immediately, precisely because there is no depth. Enthusiasm arrives early and leaves early. And the thorns never argue with the word; they just crowd it out. Cares and riches do not debate. They take up room.

The wheat and the weeds is the one people find hardest. The servants want to pull. Anyone who loves the field wants to pull. And the answer is no, because that darnel looks almost exactly like wheat until the heads form, and pulling early costs wheat. He is not indifferent to the weeds. He is unwilling to lose the wheat to get them.

Then two small things: a seed and a bit of yeast. One grows where you can see it, one works where you cannot. And then two men, one who trips over treasure by accident and one who has been searching for good pearls his whole career. Different routes, same response: sell everything, and do it with joy. Nobody in those two parables is making a sacrifice. They are both getting a bargain.

And then home. Nazareth. Where they get every fact right, the carpenter's son, Mary, the brothers by name, and conclude precisely the wrong thing. Familiarity did not give them an advantage. It gave them a category He would not fit in.
The last verse is the one to sit with. He did not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief. Not could not, because the power ran out. Would not, in a place that had already decided.

verses.1: On that day Jesus went out of the house, and sat by the seaside.
verses.2: Great multitudes gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat, and sat, and all the multitude stood on the beach.
verses.3: He spoke to them many things in parables, saying, “Behold, a farmer went out to sow.
verses.4: As he sowed, some seeds fell by the roadside, and the birds came and devoured them.
verses.5: Others fell on rocky ground, where they didn’t have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth of earth.
verses.6: When the sun had risen, they were scorched. Because they had no root, they withered away.
verses.7: Others fell among thorns. The thorns grew up and choked them.
verses.8: Others fell on good soil, and yielded fruit: some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.
verses.9: He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
verses.10: The disciples came, and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?”
verses.11: He answered them, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is not given to them.
verses.12: For whoever has, to him will be given, and he will have abundance, but whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he has.
verses.13: Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they don’t see, and hearing, they don’t hear, neither do they understand.
verses.14: In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says, ‘By hearing you will hear, and will in no way understand; Seeing you will see, and will in no way perceive:
verses.15: for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again; and I would heal them.’
verses.16: “But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear.
verses.17: For most certainly I tell you that many prophets and righteous men desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them; and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.
verses.18: “Hear, then, the parable of the farmer.
verses.19: When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside.
verses.20: What was sown on the rocky places, this is he who hears the word, and immediately with joy receives it;
verses.21: yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he stumbles.
verses.22: What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful.
verses.23: What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.”
verses.24: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field,
verses.25: but while people slept, his enemy came and sowed darnel weeds also among the wheat, and went away.
verses.26: But when the blade sprang up and produced fruit, then the darnel weeds appeared also.
verses.27: The servants of the householder came and said to him, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where did these darnel weeds come from?’
verses.28: “He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ “The servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and gather them up?’
verses.29: “But he said, ‘No, lest perhaps while you gather up the darnel weeds, you root up the wheat with them.
verses.30: Let both grow together until the harvest, and in the harvest time I will tell the reapers, “First, gather up the darnel weeds, and bind them in bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”
verses.31: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field;
verses.32: which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs, and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches.”
verses.33: He spoke another parable to them. “The Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, until it was all leavened.”
verses.34: Jesus spoke all these things in parables to the multitudes; and without a parable, he didn’t speak to them,
verses.35: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying, “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.”
verses.36: Then Jesus sent the multitudes away, and went into the house. His disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the darnel weeds of the field.”
verses.37: He answered them, “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man,
verses.38: the field is the world; and the good seed, these are the children of the Kingdom; and the darnel weeds are the children of the evil one.
verses.39: The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
verses.40: As therefore the darnel weeds are gathered up and burned with fire; so will it be at the end of this age.
verses.41: The Son of Man will send out his angels, and they will gather out of his Kingdom all things that cause stumbling, and those who do iniquity,
verses.42: and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth.
verses.43: Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.
verses.44: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found, and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field.
verses.45: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a merchant seeking fine pearls,
verses.46: who having found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
verses.47: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a dragnet, that was cast into the sea, and gathered some fish of every kind,
verses.48: which, when it was filled, they drew up on the beach. They sat down, and gathered the good into containers, but the bad they threw away.
verses.49: So will it be in the end of the world. The angels will come and separate the wicked from among the righteous,
verses.50: and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be the weeping and the gnashing of teeth.”
verses.51: Jesus said to them, “Have you understood all these things?” They answered him, “Yes, Lord.”
verses.52: He said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been made a disciple in the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a householder, who brings out of his treasure new and old things.”
verses.53: When Jesus had finished these parables, he departed from there.
verses.54: Coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom, and these mighty works?
verses.55: Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t his mother called Mary, and his brothers, James, Joses, Simon, and Judas?
verses.56: Aren’t all of his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all of these things?”
verses.57: They were offended by him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country, and in his own house.”
verses.58: He didn’t do many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 14 - A Head on a Platter, Twelve Baskets Left Over, and a Walk in the Fourth Watch
chapters.title: A Head on a Platter, Twelve Baskets Left Over, and a Walk in the Fourth Watch
keyNotes: Herod's guilty conscience supplies the chapter's opening theory: this is John, risen. Guilt produces its own theology (Matthew 14:2).
John was imprisoned for telling a king that his marriage was unlawful - a matter Leviticus addresses directly (Matthew 14:3-4).
Herod wanted him dead already and was restrained only by fear of the crowd, not by conscience (Matthew 14:5).
The oath is the hinge. He kills a prophet rather than look weak in front of dinner guests (Matthew 14:9).
Matthew tells the whole story as a flashback, triggered by Herod hearing about Yahshua. The shadow of it falls across everything that follows (Matthew 14:1-12).
"They went and told Jesus" - John's disciples bring the news to Him personally (Matthew 14:12).
His response to the news is to withdraw to a deserted place. He is grieving, and the crowd follows Him into it (Matthew 14:13).
He does not send them away. He has compassion and heals their sick, on the day He heard His cousin had been beheaded (Matthew 14:14).
"You give them something to eat" is an assignment given to men who have just explained that they cannot (Matthew 14:16).
The miracle passes through their hands. He blesses and breaks; the disciples distribute (Matthew 14:19).
Twelve baskets left over - one for each of the men who said it could not be done (Matthew 14:20).
The count is five thousand men "besides women and children," so the crowd was considerably larger than the number given (Matthew 14:21).
He makes them get into the boat and sends them into the wind. The storm is not an accident of scheduling (Matthew 14:22).
Then He goes up the mountain alone to pray - the response to grief He was interrupted from hours earlier (Matthew 14:23).
The fourth watch is roughly three to six in the morning. They had been fighting the wind most of the night before He came (Matthew 14:25).
"It is I" renders ego eimi - the same words as I AM. What He says to calm them is a name (Matthew 14:27).
Peter asks for a command, not permission. "Command me to come" - and he does walk (Matthew 14:28-29).
He sinks when he looks at the wind, and the reach is immediate. The rebuke comes after the hand, not before it (Matthew 14:30-31).
The chapter ends where chapter 9 did - people reaching for the fringe of His garment (Matthew 14:36).

intro: The disciples do something very human in verse 1. They have just walked out of the hardest confrontation of His ministry, and they change the subject to architecture. Look at the buildings. To be fair, the buildings were astonishing; some of Herod's stones weigh hundreds of tons and are still in the retaining wall today.

But the chapter opens on a guilty man's theology. Herod hears about Yahshua and concludes it must be John come back from the dead. Guilt is inventive that way. And then Matthew backs up and tells us why Herod's conscience is in that state.

The detail worth stopping on is verse 9. The king was grieved. He did not want to do it. And he did it anyway, for the sake of his oaths, and of those who sat at the table with him. A prophet died because a man would not look foolish in front of his dinner guests. Rash words and an audience have killed more than anyone likes to count.

Then verse 12: John's disciples buried the body, and then they went and told Yahshua. And verse 13: when He heard it, He withdrew to a deserted place apart. He is grieving. He wants to be alone. That is the emotional weather of everything that follows.

And the crowd follows Him into it. On foot, around the lake, thousands of them, into His grief, and He does not send them away. He goes out, sees them, is moved with compassion, and heals their sick. On the day He found out His cousin had been beheaded.

Then "you give them something to eat," said to men who have just carefully explained that they have five loaves and two fish. The miracle passes through their hands, He blesses and breaks, they distribute, and at the end there are twelve baskets left over. One each.

Then He makes them get into the boat. That word matters; the storm is not bad luck. And He finally gets the solitude He wanted, up the mountain, alone, praying, and while He prays they are fighting a headwind for most of the night. He comes in the fourth watch, which is three in the morning at the earliest. He was not late. He came at the hour He meant to.

And when He speaks, the words are ego eimi, it is I, or I AM. He calms them with a name before He calms the wind. Then notice the order in verses 30 and 31. Peter sinks. He cries out. Immediately Yahshua stretches out His hand and takes hold of him, and then asks why he doubted. The hand comes first. The question comes once he is safe.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 15 - Washed Hands, a Canaanite Woman, and Seven Baskets in Gentile Country
chapters.title: Washed Hands, a Canaanite Woman, and Seven Baskets in Gentile Country
keyNotes: The delegation comes from Jerusalem. This is not a local complaint; head office has sent people (Matthew 15:1).
The charge concerns the tradition of the elders, not the written Torah. Hand-washing before meals was a rabbinic requirement, not a Mosaic one (Matthew 15:2).
His counter-charge is heavier than the charge: you break the commandment of God by your tradition (Matthew 15:3).
The example is corban - money declared devoted to God and thereby withheld from ageing parents. Piety used as a legal instrument to avoid an obligation (Matthew 15:5-6).
"You have made the commandment of God void because of your tradition" is the sentence the whole exchange turns on (Matthew 15:6).
Isaiah 29 is quoted almost verbatim: near with the mouth, far in the heart, worship taught by the rules of men (Matthew 15:8-9).
"That which enters the mouth doesn't defile" is said in the specific context of unwashed hands - verse 20 makes the subject explicit (Matthew 15:11, 20).
The disciples' concern is that the Pharisees were offended. His answer is that some plants are not going to survive anyway (Matthew 15:12-13).
"Blind guides of the blind" is a warning about who is leading, not only about who is lost (Matthew 15:14).
The defilement list is all relational - murders, adulteries, thefts, false testimony. What comes out of the heart lands on other people (Matthew 15:19).
He then walks north into Gentile territory, Tyre and Sidon - the very region He pronounced woe over in chapter 11 (Matthew 15:21).
The Canaanite woman uses a Jewish messianic title: son of David. She knows exactly whom she is addressing (Matthew 15:22).
He answers her not a word, and then answers with a restriction, and then with a hard illustration. Three refusals, and she stays (Matthew 15:23-26).
The word for dogs here is the diminutive - household dogs under a table rather than strays in the street. She hears the opening and takes it (Matthew 15:26-27).
She does not dispute the illustration; she extends it. Yes, Lord - and even the dogs eat the crumbs (Matthew 15:27).
"Woman, great is your faith" is said only twice in this Gospel, both times to a Gentile - here and to the centurion (Matthew 15:28, 8:10).
The crowd that follows glorifies "the God of Israel," which is how Gentiles would say it (Matthew 15:31).
The second feeding is not a repeat. Seven loaves, four thousand, seven baskets, and it happens on the Gentile side of the lake (Matthew 15:32-38).
The disciples ask the same question they asked in chapter 14 - where would we get bread. Having seen it once does not appear to help (Matthew 15:33).

intro: Be precise about what is being argued here, because it is easy to hear this chapter as bigger than it is. The delegation from Jerusalem does not accuse the disciples of breaking Torah. They accuse them of breaking the tradition of the elders, a rabbinic requirement to wash hands before eating, which Moses never gave. And Yahshua's counter is not that tradition is worthless. It is that this tradition has been used to cancel a commandment.

The example He picks is devastating. Corban: you declare your assets devoted to God, and therefore unavailable to your ageing father and mother. The commandment says honour them. The workaround says the money is God's now. Religion arranged so that it removes an obligation instead of creating one.

Then Isaiah 29, quoted almost word for word. Near with the mouth. Far in the heart. Worship taught by the rules of men. That verse was written about people in the temple, and He hands it straight to the people running it.

The disciples' reaction is worth noticing; they are worried the Pharisees took offence. His answer is not conciliatory. Every plant the Father did not plant will be pulled up. Leave them alone. And then: they are blind guides of the blind. The danger is not just being lost. It is being led.

Then look at the geography. He walks north, out of Israel, into Tyre and Sidon, the exact region He pronounced woe over four chapters ago. And a Canaanite woman, the old word, the word for the people Israel was sent to drive out, calls Him son of David. She uses the Jewish messianic title.

What happens next is hard, and it is meant to be. He says nothing. Then He states a restriction. Then He gives an illustration about children's bread and dogs. Three refusals. And she does not argue with the illustration; she works inside it. Yes, Lord, and even the dogs eat the crumbs. The word He used was for household dogs, under the table, not strays in the road, and she heard the opening in it and walked through.
"Woman, great is your faith." He says that to two people in this whole Gospel, and both of them are Gentiles.

The last scene is worth watching for where it happens. He feeds four thousand on the Gentile side of the lake, and the crowd glorifies the God of Israel, which is how outsiders would put it. And notice the disciples' question in verse 33: where would we get enough bread out here? They asked that one chapter ago and watched the answer. People forget faster than they like to admit.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 16 - Who Do You Say That I Am, and a Confession Followed by a Rebuke
chapters.title: Who Do You Say That I Am, and a Confession Followed by a Rebuke
keyNotes: Pharisees and Sadducees arrive together, which almost never happened. They agreed on very little except opposing Him (Matthew 16:1).
They want a sign from heaven after a chapter in which four thousand people were fed. The problem was never the evidence (Matthew 16:1).
The weather proverb is the sting: you can read the sky and you cannot read the times you are standing in (Matthew 16:2-3).
The only sign offered is Jonah, again. He gives them the same answer He gave in chapter 12 and then leaves (Matthew 16:4).
The disciples hear "yeast" and think about lunch. Their instinct under correction is to assume they are in trouble about logistics (Matthew 16:7).
His frustration is specifically about memory - do you not remember the five loaves, the seven loaves, the baskets (Matthew 16:9-10).
Yeast is teaching. A very small amount of wrong doctrine changes the whole batch quietly (Matthew 16:12).
Caesarea Philippi sits at the base of a cliff full of niches for pagan gods, beside a cave called the gates of Hades. He asks the question there deliberately (Matthew 16:13).
The crowd's guesses are all flattering and all wrong - John, Elijah, Jeremiah, a prophet. Being highly regarded is not the same as being known (Matthew 16:14).
"But who do you say that I am" is the hinge of the Gospel, and the pronoun is emphatic (Matthew 16:15).
Peter's confession has two halves: the Christ, and the Son of the living God. Office and identity together (Matthew 16:16).
"Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you" makes the confession a gift rather than an achievement (Matthew 16:17).
The keys language echoes Isaiah 22, where a steward is given the key of the house of David - an office of household administration, not ownership (Matthew 16:19).
Binding and loosing were rabbinic terms for declaring what was forbidden and permitted (Matthew 16:19).
"From that time" marks the turn of the whole book: from that point He begins telling them He must die (Matthew 16:21).
Peter goes from receiving revelation to being called Satan within six verses. The same man, the same day (Matthew 16:22-23).
The rebuke's content is precise: not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men. Peter's error is a good intention aimed at the wrong thing (Matthew 16:23).
The cross is named as a condition of following before it is ever named as a means of saving (Matthew 16:24).
"What will a man give in exchange for his life" is a market question with no available currency (Matthew 16:26).

intro: Two groups walk up together in verse 1 who could hardly stand each other. Pharisees believed in resurrection, angels, the oral tradition; Sadducees believed in none of it. They have found one thing to agree on. And they want a sign, one chapter after four thousand people ate from seven loaves. The issue was never the amount of evidence.

His answer is a jab at something they were good at. You look at a red sky and tell everyone what tomorrow holds. You cannot read the season you are actually living in. Then He gives them Jonah again, and leaves.

In the boat the disciples hear "beware the yeast" and immediately conclude they are being told off about forgotten bread. And His frustration is not that they are slow. It is that they do not remember. Five loaves, five thousand, twelve baskets. Seven loaves, four thousand, seven baskets. He asks them to count.

Then the location, which is doing work. Caesarea Philippi sits under a cliff face carved with niches for pagan gods, beside a deep cave the locals called the gate of the underworld. He walks His disciples into the most spiritually crowded place in the region and asks: who do people say that I am?

The answers are all complimentary and all wrong. John. Elijah. Jeremiah. A prophet. Then He narrows it, but who do you say that I am, and Peter gets it right, and is told plainly that he did not work it out. Flesh and blood did not reveal this. The confession is a gift.

And then verse 21, which turns the whole book. From that time, He began to show them that He must go to Jerusalem and be killed. Peter, still warm from the commendation, takes Him aside to correct Him, and hears "get behind me, Satan." Notice the reason given. Not that Peter was malicious, but that he was setting his mind on the things of men. He wanted a good thing. He wanted his friend not to die.

Hold verse 24 next to verse 22. Peter says this will never happen to you. And the next words out of Yahshua's mouth are: if anyone wants to come after me, let him take up his cross. The thing Peter wanted to spare Him is the thing He hands to everyone who follows.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 17 - A Face Like the Sun, a Boy His Disciples Could Not Help, and a Coin in a Fish
chapters.title: A Face Like the Sun, a Boy His Disciples Could Not Help, and a Coin in a Fish
keyNotes: "After six days" ties the mountain directly to the confession and the first passion prediction. It is the answer to what they have just been told (Matthew 17:1).
Peter, James and John are the same three taken into Jairus's house and later into Gethsemane (Matthew 17:1).
Moses' face shone because he had been with God; here the light comes from inside (Matthew 17:2, Exodus 34:29).
Moses died and was buried by God with no known grave; Elijah left in a whirlwind. Both are unusual departures, and both men are standing there (Matthew 17:3).
Peter's instinct is to build three shelters - and the word is the one used for the booths of Sukkot, the feast of tents (Matthew 17:4).
The cloud is the same cloud that covered Sinai and filled the tabernacle. It is not weather (Matthew 17:5).
The voice adds three words it did not say at the Jordan: listen to him. That is the correction of Peter's three-tents proposal (Matthew 17:5).
They fall on their faces at the voice, not at the light. Hearing was more frightening than seeing (Matthew 17:6).
He touches them. That is His habit - lepers, the blind, the dead, and now three terrified friends (Matthew 17:7).
"They saw no one, except Jesus alone" is Matthew's quiet answer to the three-tents idea (Matthew 17:8).
The Elijah question comes down the mountain with them, and He identifies John as the fulfilment - and immediately connects John's treatment to His own coming suffering (Matthew 17:12).
From the mountain to a father on his knees. The transfiguration is one paragraph; the failure at the bottom of the hill is longer (Matthew 17:14-16).
"They could not cure him" - these are men who had been given authority over unclean spirits in chapter 10 (Matthew 17:16).
The rebuke "faithless and perverse generation" is aimed broadly, not only at the nine (Matthew 17:17).
The private question - why could we not - gets a private answer: because of your unbelief (Matthew 17:19-20).
A mustard seed is the measure. The issue is not the quantity of faith but whether there is any (Matthew 17:20).
The second passion prediction is shorter and blunter, and their response this time is sorrow rather than argument (Matthew 17:22-23).
The didrachma was the temple tax of Exodus 30 - a half shekel for the upkeep of the sanctuary, not a Roman tax (Matthew 17:24).
The argument He makes is that a king's own son does not pay his father's tax. It is a claim about whose house the temple is (Matthew 17:25-26).
And having established the exemption, He pays it anyway - lest we cause them to stumble (Matthew 17:27).
The coin covers two people. He includes Peter in the exemption and in the payment (Matthew 17:27).

intro: Start with the first three words: after six days. Six days after what? After Peter's confession and after Yahshua told them for the first time that He was going to Jerusalem to die. They have had most of a week to sit with the worst news they had ever been given, and then He takes three of them up a mountain and lets them see who they have been walking beside.
Moses' face shone once, in Exodus 34, because he had been standing in the presence of God. Here the light is not reflected. It comes out from inside Him.

And the two men standing there are worth noticing. Moses, whom God buried Himself in a grave nobody has ever found. Elijah, who left in a whirlwind without dying. The law and the prophets, both with strange endings, both talking with Him.

Peter's suggestion is not silly, and it is not greedy. He wants to build three booths, and the word is the one used for Sukkot, because if Moses and Elijah are here then surely this is the great day, and you build shelters for the great day. His mistake is the arithmetic. Three tents means three equals. The voice from the cloud corrects it in four words: listen to him. Not to them. To him. And when they look up, only Yahshua is there.

Then straight down the mountain into a mess. A father on his knees, a boy who falls into fire and water, and nine disciples who could not do anything about it, men who had been given authority over exactly this in chapter 10. The glory lasted a paragraph. The failure gets more verses.

Their question afterward is honest and private: why could we not? And the answer is not that they lacked technique. It was unbelief. And the measure He gives is deliberately small, a mustard seed. He is not asking for great faith. He is asking whether there is any.

The last scene is easy to skip. The temple tax is not Rome's; it is the half shekel of Exodus 30, for the upkeep of the sanctuary. And His argument is that kings do not tax their own sons, which is a claim about whose house that building is. He establishes that He does not owe it. And then He pays it anyway, so as not to make anyone stumble. Being right about an exemption and insisting on it are two different things.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 18 - A Child in the Middle, One Sheep Off the Hill, and a Debt Nobody Could Pay
chapters.title: A Child in the Middle, One Sheep Off the Hill, and a Debt Nobody Could Pay
keyNotes: The question "who is greatest" comes immediately after the temple tax and the second passion prediction. The timing is its own commentary (Matthew 18:1).
He does not answer with a name. He puts a child in the middle of the circle (Matthew 18:2).
A child in that world had no legal standing and no social weight. The point is not innocence but insignificance (Matthew 18:3-4).
"Unless you turn" is a reversal, not a refinement. The direction they are travelling is wrong (Matthew 18:3).
The millstone is the large kind, turned by a donkey rather than by hand. The image is deliberately excessive (Matthew 18:6).
Verse 7 concedes that occasions of stumbling will come, and still holds the person responsible through whom they come (Matthew 18:7).
The hand, foot and eye language is repeated from the Sermon on the Mount, but here it is set in a passage about harming others (Matthew 18:8-9).
"Their angels always see the face of my Father" is the reason given for not despising them. The little ones have standing in the throne room (Matthew 18:10).
In this telling of the lost sheep, the sheep is a believer who wandered, not an outsider. The context is people inside the community (Matthew 18:12).
The shepherd's joy is comparative and unembarrassed: more over the one than over the ninety-nine (Matthew 18:13).
"Not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish" is the summary of the whole discourse so far (Matthew 18:14).
The correction procedure begins privately and expands only as far as it has to. Every stage is aimed at gaining the brother, not at winning (Matthew 18:15-17).
"Let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector" is worth reading in this Gospel, written by a tax collector, about a man who ate with them (Matthew 18:17).
The binding and loosing of chapter 16 is repeated here to the whole community, in the context of restoring people (Matthew 18:18).
"Where two or three are gathered" sits inside a paragraph about discipline and reconciliation, not about small attendance (Matthew 18:20).
Peter's seven was generous. Rabbinic practice suggested three. He doubles it and adds one, and is still thinking in numbers (Matthew 18:21).
Seventy times seven is not a higher ceiling. It is the removal of the ledger (Matthew 18:22).
Ten thousand talents is an absurd figure - more than the annual tax revenue of whole provinces. The debt is unpayable on purpose (Matthew 18:24).
A hundred denarii is about a third of a year's wage - a real debt, not a trivial one. The contrast is not between large and nothing (Matthew 18:28).
The two men use almost identical words: have patience with me and I will repay. One is heard, one is not (Matthew 18:26, 29).
The parable's charge is not that the servant failed to forgive, but that he had already been forgiven and still would not (Matthew 18:32-33).
"From your hearts" closes the discourse. The standard is not a procedure completed but a debt actually released (Matthew 18:35).

intro: Look at when they ask it. He has just told them, for the second time, that He is going to be handed over and killed. And the conversation they are having is about which of them ranks highest. That is not a caricature of the disciples; that is most people, most weeks.

He does not name anyone. He calls a child over and stands him in the middle. And the point is easy to sentimentalise. In that world a child was not a symbol of innocence. A child had no legal standing, no property, no vote, no leverage. Yahshua puts the least significant person in the room in the centre of an argument about significance.

Then the tone hardens fast. A millstone, and the word is the large one, the kind a donkey turns, around the neck, in the depths of the sea, as the preferable outcome for someone who trips up one of these little ones. He is not gentle about people who damage the vulnerable.

And the lost sheep here is not the one in Luke 15. There the sheep is an outsider. Here it is one of these little ones, somebody inside, who wandered. The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine on the hills, and rejoices more over the one, and it is not the will of the Father that even one of them be lost.

That is the setting for verses 15 to 17, and it changes how they read. The procedure is not a disciplinary escalation designed to remove people. Every step is the smallest step that might work: alone first, then one or two, then the assembly. And the stated goal is you have gained back your brother. Even the last line, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector, lands strangely in a Gospel written by a tax collector, about a man who kept eating with them.

Then Peter, doing arithmetic. The rabbis suggested three times; he offers seven and is probably pleased with himself. And seventy times seven is not a bigger number to reach. It is the end of counting.

Then the parable, and the two figures matter. Ten thousand talents was more than the yearly taxes of entire provinces, an amount chosen because no one could ever pay it. A hundred denarii was about four months' wages, not nothing, a real debt someone would resent. The second man's offence was genuine. That is the point.

Both debtors say almost exactly the same sentence: have patience with me and I will repay. One of them is heard. The charge against the servant is not that forgiveness is hard. It is that he had already received it and still took his neighbour by the throat.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 19 - One Flesh, Little Children, and a Young Man Who Walked Away Sad
chapters.title: One Flesh, Little Children, and a Young Man Who Walked Away Sad
keyNotes: Chapter 19 opens with a geographical turn - out of Galilee, toward Judea. From here the whole Gospel is a journey to Jerusalem (Matthew 19:1).

The divorce question is a live rabbinic dispute. The school of Shammai allowed it for unfaithfulness; the school of Hillel for almost anything. "For any reason" is Hillel's phrase, and they want Him to pick a side (Matthew 19:3).
He refuses the terms of the question and goes back behind Moses to Genesis. Design before concession (Matthew 19:4-5).
"What God has joined together" makes marriage an act of God rather than only a contract between two people (Matthew 19:6).
The Pharisees say Moses commanded; He corrects it to allowed. Deuteronomy 24 regulates a practice, it does not institute one (Matthew 19:7-8).
"Because of the hardness of your hearts" locates the problem in people, not in the provision (Matthew 19:8).
The disciples' reaction - better not to marry - is not admirable, and He does not endorse it. He says not everyone can receive this (Matthew 19:10-11).
The three kinds of eunuch cover birth, injury and choice. Only the third is voluntary, and it is described as for the Kingdom's sake (Matthew 19:12).
The disciples rebuke people for bringing children after being told two chapters ago to receive one in His name. They forget quickly, as do we (Matthew 19:13, 18:5).
"Why do you call me good" is not a denial. It is a question that invites the young man to follow his own word to its conclusion (Matthew 19:17).
The commandments He lists are all from the second table - the ones about neighbours - plus love your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 19:18-19).
The one commandment conspicuously absent from the list is the tenth: you shall not covet. It is the one the next instruction tests (Matthew 19:18-21).
"What do I still lack" is an honest question from a man who senses that keeping the rules has not settled anything (Matthew 19:20).
The instruction to sell is given to this man, not to every man. But nobody should relax too quickly - he went away sad, and He let him go (Matthew 19:21-22).
The camel and the needle is deliberate hyperbole. The disciples understood it as impossible, which is why they asked who then can be saved (Matthew 19:24-25).
Their astonishment assumes wealth is a sign of blessing. He does not correct the premise so much as dismantle the confidence (Matthew 19:25).
"With God all things are possible" is the answer to salvation being impossible - including for the rich (Matthew 19:26).
Peter's "what then will we have" is transactional, and He answers it generously before correcting it in the next chapter (Matthew 19:27-30).

intro: The question in verse 3 is not innocent, and it is not abstract. There were two rabbinic schools arguing about this. Shammai said a man could divorce his wife only for unfaithfulness. Hillel said for almost anything; a spoiled meal was the standing example. "For any reason" is Hillel's actual phrase. They are asking Him to join a party.

And He will not. He goes back behind Moses altogether, past the concession in Deuteronomy, to the design in Genesis. Male and female. One flesh. And then the sentence that reframes the entire subject: what God has joined together. Which makes a marriage something God did, not only something two people signed.

Notice the correction in verse 8. They said Moses commanded. He says Moses allowed, because of hardness of heart. Deuteronomy 24 was never establishing divorce; it was limiting the damage of something already happening.

Then the disciples, who react to all this by concluding that marriage is not worth it, which is not a spiritual response, and He does not treat it as one. And then children are brought to Him, and the disciples push them away, two chapters after being told that whoever receives one such child receives Him. Everyone is quicker to forget than they like to think.

The young man is the part of this chapter that stays with people. He is sincere. He asks a real question. He has kept the commandments, and Yahshua does not dispute that. And when Yahshua lists the commandments, He gives the ones about how you treat other people, and leaves out the tenth. You shall not covet. And then the next thing He says tests exactly that one.
Then the hardest line in the chapter: he went away sad. And Yahshua let him go. He did not chase him. He did not soften the terms. And in Mark's telling, He loved him while He said it.

The camel and the needle is meant to sound impossible, and the disciples heard it that way: who then can be saved. Their shock tells us they assumed wealth was evidence of God's favour. And the answer He gives is not a technique. It is that salvation is impossible for anyone, and God does the impossible.

Peter in verse 27 is doing the maths on what following has cost. He gets a generous answer and a warning in the same breath: many who are first will be last. And chapter 20 opens with a parable about exactly that.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 20 - A Denarius for Everyone, a Cup Nobody Understood, and Two Men by the Road
chapters.title: A Denarius for Everyone, a Cup Nobody Understood, and Two Men by the Road
keyNotes: The parable answers Peter's question at the end of chapter 19 and is bracketed by the same sentence at both ends: the last will be first (Matthew 19:30, 20:16).
Day labourers were the most precarious workers in that economy. Not being hired meant not eating (Matthew 20:3, 6-7).
Only the first group negotiates. Everyone after that is told "whatever is right" and goes anyway (Matthew 20:2, 4).
The eleventh hour men are not lazy. Their answer is that no one hired them (Matthew 20:7).
The owner's instruction to pay the last first is what makes the grievance possible. He arranges for the first to see it (Matthew 20:8).
The complaint is not that they were underpaid. It is that others were made equal to them (Matthew 20:12).
"Friend, I am doing you no wrong" is the whole defence: nobody received less than agreed (Matthew 20:13).
"Is your eye evil because I am good" makes generosity the offence. Grace to someone else feels like theft when we are counting (Matthew 20:15).
The third passion prediction is the most detailed yet - condemned, handed to Gentiles, mocked, scourged, crucified (Matthew 20:18-19).
It is the first time He names crucifixion for Himself (Matthew 20:19).
Immediately after that, a request for the two best seats. The proximity is the point (Matthew 20:20-21).
The mother asks, but He answers them - "you do not know what you are asking" is plural (Matthew 20:22).
The two places at His right and left will be occupied on a hill outside Jerusalem, by two criminals (Matthew 20:21, 27:38).
"You will indeed drink my cup" is a promise, not a threat. James was the first apostle killed; John outlived them all in exile (Matthew 20:23).
The ten are indignant, which suggests they wanted the same thing and were beaten to it (Matthew 20:24).
"It shall not be so among you" is a direct contrast with how the nations do authority. The structure is inverted, not softened (Matthew 20:25-26).
Verse 28 is the clearest statement in Matthew of why He came: to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many (Matthew 20:28).
The two blind men use the messianic title son of David, twice, and the crowd tries to silence them (Matthew 20:30-31).
"What do you want me to do for you" is the same question He asked the mother of James and John eight verses earlier. Two very different answers (Matthew 20:21, 32).
He touched their eyes. The healing is done by hand, not at a distance (Matthew 20:34).

intro: This parable is an answer. Peter has just asked what they will get for having left everything, and the last line of chapter 19 and the last line of the parable are the same sentence. Everything in between is Yahshua explaining what is wrong with the question.

Understand who these men are. Day labourers were the bottom of that economy: no land, no trade, no security. Standing in the marketplace at five in the afternoon means you have stood there all day and nobody wanted you. And when the owner asks why they are idle, their answer is not laziness. Nobody hired us.

Notice too that only the first group negotiates a price. Everyone after that is told "whatever is right" and goes on that alone. The first group works for a contract; the rest work on the owner's character.
And then the detail that makes the whole story go: he tells the foreman to pay the last ones first. He arranges for the men who worked all day to watch. He wants them to see it.

The complaint in verse 12 is worth reading slowly, because it is not what most people assume. They do not say we were cheated. They say you have made them equal to us. That is the grievance. And the answer, is your eye evil because I am good, puts generosity itself on trial. Grace given to somebody else can feel like something taken away, if a ledger is being kept.

Then the third time He tells them He is going to die, and this time He says the word: crucify. And the very next verse is a mother asking for the two best seats in the Kingdom for her boys. Matthew puts those side by side deliberately. And there is a shadow over the request that nobody in the room can see yet, because when He is finally lifted up there will be a man on His right and a man on His left, and they will both be thieves.
The other ten are furious, which almost certainly means they wanted it too and someone else's mother got there first.

Verse 28 is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward. Not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many. And then He stops on a road for two blind men that everybody else was trying to shut up, and asks them the exact question He asked James and John's mother: what do you want me to do for you. Two answers. Only one of them He could grant.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 21 - A Borrowed Donkey, Tables on the Floor, and a Vineyard with Murderous Tenants
chapters.title: A Borrowed Donkey, Tables on the Floor, and a Vineyard with Murderous Tenants
keyNotes: He arranges the entry deliberately - the donkey, the route, the timing. This is the one moment He stops avoiding public acclaim (Matthew 21:2-5).
A king riding a donkey rather than a horse is a specific image: coming in peace rather than to make war (Matthew 21:5).
Zechariah 9:9 is quoted with the doubled phrasing of Hebrew poetry - a donkey, a colt the foal of a donkey - which is one animal described twice (Matthew 21:5).
Hosanna is not originally praise. It is a plea: save us now, from Psalm 118 (Matthew 21:9).
The city asks "who is this" and the crowd answers with the lowest available title: the prophet from Nazareth. Days later this crowd will be shouting something else (Matthew 21:10-11).
The trade He overturns took place in the Court of the Gentiles - the only part of the temple a non-Jew could enter (Matthew 21:12).
The two quotations He fuses come from Isaiah 56 and Jeremiah 7. Isaiah says "a house of prayer for all peoples"; Matthew leaves that phrase out, but the location makes the point (Matthew 21:13).
"A den of robbers" is Jeremiah's phrase for a temple people treat as a safe house between sins (Matthew 21:13).
The first thing that happens in the cleared temple is that the blind and the lame come in and are healed - people traditionally kept at a distance from it (Matthew 21:14).
The chief priests are indignant about the children shouting, not about the trading He stopped (Matthew 21:15).
The fig tree is the only destructive miracle in the Gospels, and it is aimed at something with leaves and no fruit - the display without the substance (Matthew 21:19).
In that region a fig tree in leaf should already carry early fruit. Leaves without figs is a false advertisement (Matthew 21:19).
The authority question is the leadership's official challenge, and He answers with a question they cannot afford to answer honestly (Matthew 21:23-27).
Their reasoning in verses 25 and 26 is entirely about consequences. Truth does not enter into it (Matthew 21:25-26).
"We don't know" is a lie, and He declines to give them anything more (Matthew 21:27).
The two sons turn on the difference between saying and doing - the same test as the two houses in chapter 7 (Matthew 21:28-31).
Tax collectors and prostitutes entering ahead of them is not a compliment to sin; it is a statement about who actually repented (Matthew 21:31-32).
The vineyard parable is built out of Isaiah 5 - the hedge, the winepress, the tower - so the audience knows exactly who the vineyard is before the story moves (Matthew 21:33).
The servants sent and beaten are the prophets. The son sent last is unmistakable, and they understood it (Matthew 21:35-39, 45).
The tenants kill the heir in order to seize the inheritance - which is a plan that only makes sense if you think the owner is never coming back (Matthew 21:38).
They pronounce their own sentence in verse 41 before realising the parable is about them (Matthew 21:41, 45).
The stone of Psalm 118 is the same psalm the crowd was singing at the entry, twenty verses earlier (Matthew 21:42, 9).

intro: For most of this Gospel He has told people to keep quiet. Now He arranges a public entrance down to the detail: which village, which animal, what to say if anyone asks. He is not swept along by a crowd. He is staging something, and He is staging it out of Zechariah.
And the animal matters. A king coming home from war rode a horse. A king coming in peace rode a donkey. Everyone lining that road knew the difference.

So does the word they are shouting. Hosanna is not a cheer. It is Psalm 118: save us now, we beg you. They are asking for a rescue, and they are almost certainly picturing Rome. Then the city asks who is this, and the crowd gives the smallest answer available: the prophet, from Nazareth, in Galilee. Within the week, some of these same voices will be shouting something different.

Then the temple. And it matters where the tables were. The buying and selling happened in the Court of the Gentiles, the one part of that building a non-Jew was allowed to stand in. The only space set aside for the nations had been turned into a market. And the verse He quotes, Isaiah 56, says my house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.

The other half of the quotation is Jeremiah's: a den of robbers. Notice what a den is. It is not where robbers rob. It is where they go afterward, to feel safe. He is saying the building had become a place people used to feel secure in between the things they were doing.

And the first thing that happens once the tables are gone: the blind and the lame come to Him in the temple, and He heals them. The people who had always been kept at arm's length from that place walk into the space He just cleared.

The fig tree in the morning is the only miracle He ever does that destroys something, and the target is precise. In that region a fig tree in leaf should already have early fruit on it. Leaves with nothing under them is a tree advertising something it does not have. He had just walked out of a temple doing the same thing.

Then the challenge, by what authority, and His counter-question about John, and their private deliberation in verses 25 and 26, which is one of the most honest paragraphs in Scripture about how people in power actually decide things. Not once do they ask what is true. They ask what each answer will cost them.

The vineyard parable comes from somewhere specific. The hedge, the winepress, the tower: that is Isaiah 5, word for word, and everyone listening knew that song and knew the vineyard was Israel. So they follow the story all the way to the end, and in verse 41 they pronounce the sentence themselves. Then verse 45: they perceived that he spoke about them.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 22 - A Feast Nobody Came To, a Coin with a Face on It, and a Question Nobody Could Answer
chapters.title: A Feast Nobody Came To, a Coin with a Face on It, and a Question Nobody Could Answer
keyNotes: This is the third vineyard-and-invitation parable in a row, and the third time the leadership is the subject (Matthew 21:28, 33, 22:2).
In that culture there were two invitations - one in advance, one when the food was ready. These guests had already accepted and then refused to come (Matthew 22:3-4).
The excuses are ordinary: a farm, a business. Nothing wicked. Just other things (Matthew 22:5).
Then the escalation - some of them killed the servants, which is the same fate the prophets met in the previous parable (Matthew 22:6).
"Both bad and good" is a startling detail. The hall is filled without a screening at the door (Matthew 22:10).
But there is a garment. Being brought in freely is not the same as coming in on your own terms (Matthew 22:11-12).
"Friend" is the same word He will use for Judas in the garden - courteous and terrible at once (Matthew 22:12, 26:50).
Pharisees and Herodians together is an unnatural alliance: one group hated Roman tax, the other depended on Roman favour (Matthew 22:16).
The flattery in verse 16 is accurate. Everything they say about Him is true, and they do not believe a word of it (Matthew 22:16).
The question is a genuine trap. Yes, and He loses the crowd; no, and He is reported to Rome (Matthew 22:17).
He does not carry the coin. He asks them to produce one, and they do - in the temple (Matthew 22:19).
The word for image is eikon, the same word used in Genesis for what humans are made in. Caesar's face is on the coin; God's image is on the man holding it (Matthew 22:20-21).
"Give to God the things that are God's" is the larger half of the sentence, and the half they did not ask about (Matthew 22:21).
The Sadducees only accepted the five books of Moses, which is why His answer comes from Exodus and not from Daniel or the Psalms (Matthew 22:23, 32).
Their riddle is built on levirate marriage - the duty of a brother to raise up offspring for the dead (Matthew 22:24).
"You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God" names both halves of the error: bad reading and small expectations (Matthew 22:29).
The whole argument turns on a present tense: I am the God of Abraham. Not was (Matthew 22:32).
The lawyer's question was a live debate - the rabbis counted 613 commandments and argued about weight (Matthew 22:36).
He answers with the Shema and with Leviticus 19:18, and says everything else hangs on those two (Matthew 22:37-40).
Then He asks His own question, and it is about identity, not ethics: whose son is the Christ (Matthew 22:42).
Psalm 110 is the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament, and He is the first to use it this way (Matthew 22:44).
"Neither did any man dare ask him any more questions" closes the public ministry (Matthew 22:46).

intro: Three parables in a row now, all aimed at the same men, and this is the third. And there is a cultural detail that makes it sharper: invitations in that world came twice. First a general notice, then a second call when the food was actually on the table. These guests had already said yes. They are not refusing an invitation; they are breaking a commitment.

And look at the reasons. A farm. A business. Nothing scandalous. That is what makes it uncomfortable. Most of what keeps people from God is not wickedness; it is other things that seemed more pressing that day. Then the story turns violent, and the servants are killed, which is exactly what happened to the servants in the parable He told an hour earlier.

The hall gets filled from the crossroads, and Matthew tells us who came: both bad and good. Nobody was screened at the door. Which makes the next paragraph land hard, because there is still a garment, and a man without one. Coming in free is not the same as coming in on your own terms. And the king calls him friend, the same word Yahshua uses for Judas in Gethsemane.

Then the delegations start arriving. Pharisees and Herodians first, and that pairing is absurd: one group loathed the Roman tax, the other lived off Roman favour. And their flattery in verse 16 is entirely accurate. You are honest, you teach truly, you are not partial. Every word true, and not one of them believed.

The trap is real. Say yes to the tax and the crowd turns; say no and He is a rebel by lunch. So He asks for a coin. Notice that He does not have one; they produce it, in the temple. And the word He uses for the image on it is eikon, which is the word Genesis uses for what human beings are made in. Caesar's face on the coin, so give it back to him. God's image on the man holding the coin, so give that back too. Everyone remembers the first half of that sentence. The second half is the one with teeth.

The Sadducees are next, with a riddle they had clearly used before. And they only accepted the five books of Moses, which is why He does not quote Daniel or the Psalms at them. He goes to the burning bush, and the whole argument hangs on a verb. I am the God of Abraham. Not I was. Those men were centuries dead and God speaks of Himself in the present tense.

Then the lawyer's question, which was a genuine rabbinic debate: 613 commandments, and which carries most weight. He gives the Shema, and then Leviticus 19:18, and says the whole law and the prophets hang on those two. Not that the rest is cancelled. That the rest hangs there.

And He gets the last question. Whose son is the Christ? They answer David's, correctly, and He asks how David can call his own descendant Lord. Nobody answers. And from that day, verse 46 says, nobody dared ask Him anything. The debating is over.

verses.6: and the rest grabbed his servants, and treated them shamefully, and killed them.
verses.7: When the king heard that, he was angry, and sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city.
verses.8: “Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding is ready, but those who were invited weren’t worthy.

verses.17: Tell us therefore, what do you think? Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?”
verses.18: But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said, “Why do you test me, you hypocrites?
verses.19: Show me the tax money.” They brought to him a denarius.

verses.22: When they heard it, they marveled, and left him, and went away.
verses.23: On that day Sadducees (those who say that there is no resurrection) came to him. They asked him,
verses.24: saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up offspring for his brother.’
verses.25: Now there were with us seven brothers. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother.

verses.29: But Jesus answered them, “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God.
verses.30: For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are like God’s angels in heaven.
verses.31: But concerning the resurrection of the dead, haven’t you read that which was spoken to you by God, saying,
verses.32: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?’ God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”
verses.33: When the multitudes heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.
verses.34: But the Pharisees, when they heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, gathered themselves together.
verses.35: One of them, a lawyer, asked him a question, testing him.
verses.36: “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?”
verses.37: Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’
verses.38: This is the first and great commandment.
verses.39: A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
verses.40: The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.”
verses.41: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question,
verses.42: saying, “What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “Of David.”
verses.43: He said to them, “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying,

verses.46: No one was able to answer him a word, neither did any man dare ask him any more questions from that day forward.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 23 - Seven Woes, Whitewashed Tombs, and a Hen Over Jerusalem
chapters.title: Seven Woes, Whitewashed Tombs, and a Hen Over Jerusalem
keyNotes: He begins by telling the crowd to do what these men teach. The authority of the seat is affirmed before the men in it are condemned (Matthew 23:2-3).
"They say, and don't do" is the charge the whole chapter unpacks (Matthew 23:3).
The burdens they bind are laid on other people's shoulders while they will not lift a finger. The complaint is not strictness; it is asymmetry (Matthew 23:4).
Phylacteries are small boxes of Scripture worn on arm and forehead from Deuteronomy 6:8. Making them broad is turning obedience into signage (Matthew 23:5).
"Call no man father" sits inside a list about titles that create distance - rabbi, father, master. The target is a class of religious professionals above the brothers (Matthew 23:8-10).
Verse 11 repeats what He said in chapter 20 and chapter 18. The greatest is the servant, again (Matthew 23:11).
Seven woes follow, in the same form as the prophets' oracles. Woe is a lament as much as a curse (Matthew 23:13-32).
Shutting the Kingdom against people is the first woe. Not entering themselves is bad; blocking the door is worse (Matthew 23:14).
The oath rules He mocks are real distinctions in the tradition - which oaths bind and which do not. The whole system exists to allow deniability (Matthew 23:16-22).
He does not abolish the tithe of herbs. He says do these and do not leave the other undone (Matthew 23:23).
Justice, mercy, faith are called the weightier matters - the phrase implies the rest still has weight (Matthew 23:23).
The gnat and the camel are both unclean animals; the joke is about straining a drink while swallowing something enormous (Matthew 23:24).
The cup cleaned outside and filthy inside is the same argument as chapter 15 - defilement comes from within (Matthew 23:25-26).
Tombs were whitewashed before Passover precisely so pilgrims would not touch them accidentally and become unclean. He is calling them a warning marker (Matthew 23:27).
Building the prophets' tombs while opposing the living prophet is the sharpest irony in the chapter (Matthew 23:29-31).
Abel is the first murder in the Hebrew Bible; Zachariah in 2 Chronicles is the last, because Chronicles closes the Hebrew canon. It is a way of saying "from Genesis to Malachi" (Matthew 23:35).
And then, without warning, the tone breaks. Jerusalem, Jerusalem - the voice changes from prosecutor to mourner (Matthew 23:37).
The hen and chicks image is maternal, and it is the last picture He gives of His own desire for that city (Matthew 23:37).
"And you would not" is the verdict, and it is about willingness rather than ability (Matthew 23:37).
"Your house is left to you desolate" - your house, not my Father's house, which is what He called it two chapters ago (Matthew 23:38, 21:13).
The chapter ends with a door left open: until you say, Blessed is he who comes (Matthew 23:39).

intro: This is the hardest chapter in the Gospel, and it is worth being careful about how it is read, because it has been misused. Two things anchor it. First, verse 3: whatever they tell you, do it. He upholds the seat before He indicts the men sitting in it. Second, verse 37, where the whole thing collapses into grief. This is not contempt. It is a lament, and the woes are the same form the prophets used, a word that mourns as much as it condemns.

The charge in verse 3 is the thesis: they say, and do not do. Everything after it is an example. And notice verse 4 carefully. The complaint is not that they were strict. It is that they laid the weight on other people and would not carry any of it themselves.

The titles in verses 8 to 10 are worth reading in context. He is not banning the word father in a family; Paul calls himself a father to the Corinthians a few decades later. He is attacking a class of religious professionals set above the brothers, people who need a title to keep a distance.

Then the woes. The first is the worst: shutting the Kingdom in people's faces. Not going in yourself is a tragedy; standing in the doorway is something else. And the oath rules in verses 16 to 22 were real. The tradition distinguished which oaths bound you and which did not, and the whole apparatus existed so that a man could sound sincere and still leave himself an exit.

Verse 23 is the one to hold on to, because He does not do what most readers expect. He does not say the tithe of the herbs was silly. He says: justice, mercy and faith, these you ought to have done, and not to have left the other undone. Both. The small things kept, and the weighty things not neglected for them.

The whitewashed tombs need a detail to land properly. Before Passover, graves were painted white, not for beauty, but as a warning, so that pilgrims coming to the feast would not brush against one and be made unclean. He is saying: you are the marker that warns people away.

And then verse 29, the sharpest irony in the book. They are building monuments to dead prophets while standing in front of a living one they are about to kill. The span from Abel to Zachariah is not random either. Abel is the first murder in Genesis, and Zachariah's is the last in 2 Chronicles, which is the final book of the Hebrew canon. He is saying: the whole Bible, front to back.

Then verse 37, where the voice changes. Jerusalem, Jerusalem. How often I would have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks. That is a mother's image, from a man about to be killed by that city. And then: and you would not. Not could not. Would not. And even after that, the last word is not the desolation. It is until. Until you say, blessed is he who comes.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 24 - Not One Stone, Birth Pains, and an Hour Nobody Knows
chapters.title: Not One Stone, Birth Pains, and an Hour Nobody Knows
keyNotes: The disciples point out the buildings, which were genuinely spectacular - Herod's stones measured many tons apiece (Matthew 24:1).
"Not one stone on another" was fulfilled in AD 70, within the lifetime of many who heard it (Matthew 24:2).
The disciples ask what they think is one question and is actually three: when, what sign, and the end of the age. The answer moves between them (Matthew 24:3).
The first instruction is not a prediction. It is a warning against being misled - repeated four times in the chapter (Matthew 24:4, 5, 11, 24).
Wars, famines and earthquakes are explicitly called "not yet" the end. He is lowering the temperature, not raising it (Matthew 24:6-8).
"Birth pains" is a deliberate image: increasing, purposeful, and ending in life rather than in death (Matthew 24:8).
The prediction of hatred and betrayal is addressed to them - you will be delivered up (Matthew 24:9).
"The love of many will grow cold" is the most quietly terrible line in the chapter, and its cause is given: lawlessness multiplied (Matthew 24:12).
The Good News preached to all nations before the end makes the mission part of the timetable rather than a delay to it (Matthew 24:14).
"The abomination of desolation" points back to Daniel, and Daniel's language had already been applied to Antiochus desecrating the temple in 167 BC (Matthew 24:15).
"Let the reader understand" is an aside to us, not to the crowd - the only such aside in the Gospel (Matthew 24:15).
The flight instructions are urgently practical: do not go back for a coat, pray it is not winter or a Sabbath (Matthew 24:16-20).
"For the sake of the chosen ones those days will be shortened" is mercy inside the catastrophe (Matthew 24:22).
The test for a false messiah is publicity: if someone says he is out in the desert or in an inner room, that alone disqualifies him (Matthew 24:23-26).
His coming is compared to lightning across the whole sky. Nobody will need to be told (Matthew 24:27).
The darkened sun and falling stars are stock prophetic language for the collapse of powers, used by Isaiah and Joel long before (Matthew 24:29).
The gathering from the four winds is the language of the exile promises - the scattered brought home (Matthew 24:31).
The fig tree parable is about reading a season, not calculating a date. Leaves mean summer is near, not which day (Matthew 24:32-33).
"Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not" is a startling claim to put beside creation itself (Matthew 24:35).
Verse 36 is the boundary on all speculation: not the angels, and - in this saying - not the Son (Matthew 24:36).
The days of Noah are not described as especially wicked here. They were eating, drinking and marrying. The problem was that they did not know (Matthew 24:38-39).
"Watch" and "be ready" are the imperatives the whole discourse lands on - four times in ten verses (Matthew 24:42-44).
The final parable makes readiness concrete: feeding the household on time. Watching turns out to look like ordinary faithfulness (Matthew 24:45-46).
The evil servant's error begins as a sentence in his heart - my lord is delaying - and ends in how he treats people (Matthew 24:48-49).

intro: The disciples do something very human in verse 1. They have just walked out of the hardest confrontation of His ministry, and they change the subject to architecture. Look at the buildings. And to be fair, the buildings were astonishing; some of Herod's stones weigh hundreds of tons and are still there in the retaining wall today.
And His answer stops them: not one stone on another. Within forty years it happened. Many of the men standing there lived to see it.

So on the Mount of Olives they ask what they think is one question and is really three. When will this happen. What is the sign of your coming. And what about the end of the age. He answers all three, and He moves between them, which is why this chapter is argued over. It is worth being honest about that rather than pretending the seams are not there.

But notice what the first instruction is. Not a prediction, a warning. Be careful that no one leads you astray. He says it four separate times. And when He does list the frightening things, wars, famines, earthquakes, He immediately adds that the end is not yet. He is lowering the temperature, not raising it. Every generation has read its own headlines into verse 7. He said in verse 6 not to.

Then verse 12, which is the hardest line in the chapter. Because lawlessness is multiplied, the love of many will grow cold. Not their doctrine. Their love. That is what the pressure does to people who are not watching.

Verse 15 has an aside in it, let the reader understand, and it is the only place in this Gospel where Matthew speaks past the crowd to whoever is holding the book. Something in that phrase was meant to be worked out later, and carefully.

The fig tree at the end is often misused. He is not saying a date can be calculated. He is saying a season can be read, the way anyone looking at a budding branch knows summer is coming without knowing which day it arrives. And then verse 36 fences the whole subject: nobody knows the day or the hour.

And look at how He describes Noah's generation. Not that they were unusually evil. Eating, drinking, marrying, giving in marriage: ordinary life. The problem was that they did not know until the water came.

The whole discourse lands not on a chart but on one word, said four times: watch. And then a parable that says exactly what watching looks like, a servant feeding the household on time. Not scanning the sky. Doing the job.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 25 - Ten Lamps, Three Servants, and a Judgment About a Cup of Water
chapters.title: Ten Lamps, Three Servants, and a Judgment About a Cup of Water
keyNotes: All three parables answer the same question the disciples asked on the mountain, and all three turn on a delay (Matthew 24:3, 25:5, 19).
All ten girls are virgins, all ten are invited, all ten have lamps, and all ten fall asleep. The only difference is the oil (Matthew 25:1-5).
Nobody is condemned for sleeping. The bridegroom was genuinely late, and sleeping was the reasonable thing to do (Matthew 25:5).
The refusal to share is not selfishness - it is a statement that some things cannot be lent. You cannot borrow someone else's readiness (Matthew 25:8-9).
"The door was shut" echoes Genesis 7, where Yahweh Himself shut Noah in (Matthew 25:10).
"I don't know you" is the same verdict as Matthew 7:23, said this time to people who were waiting for Him (Matthew 25:12).
A talent was an enormous sum - roughly twenty years of a labourer's wages. Even the one-talent servant was trusted with a fortune (Matthew 25:15).
The distribution is explicitly unequal and explicitly deliberate: to each according to his own ability (Matthew 25:15).
The two who traded are commended in identical words. The reward is not scaled to the return (Matthew 25:21, 23).
The third servant's stated motive is fear, and his description of his master is the opposite of what the other two experienced (Matthew 25:24-25).
His sin is not losing the money. It is doing nothing with it (Matthew 25:25-27).
The sheep and goats scene is not a parable - it is a description, and it is the last teaching before the passion (Matthew 25:31).
Sheep and goats grazed together in that country and were separated at evening. The image is one of ordinary indistinguishable mixture (Matthew 25:32).
The list is startlingly plain: food, drink, welcome, clothing, care, visitation. No religious act appears in it (Matthew 25:35-36).
Both groups are surprised. Neither the sheep nor the goats knew whom they were serving or failing to serve (Matthew 25:37-39, 44).
The goats are not condemned for cruelty but for absence - for what they did not do (Matthew 25:42-43).
"The least of these my brothers" is the hinge of every argument about this passage; His identification with them is the point either way (Matthew 25:40).
The fire is described as prepared for the devil and his angels - not for people (Matthew 25:41).

intro: Three parables, and all three are about a delay. That is not incidental; it is the whole problem the disciples had raised on the mountain. The bridegroom is late. The master is gone a long time. The Son of Man comes, but not yet.

Start with what the ten girls have in common, because it is nearly everything. All ten are virgins. All ten are invited. All ten have lamps. All ten go out to meet him. And all ten fall asleep, and notice that nobody is ever blamed for sleeping. He really was late. Sleeping was sensible. The single difference is a flask of oil.

And when the foolish ask to borrow some, the answer sounds harsh until you see what it is actually saying. There are things that cannot be lent. Nobody can borrow somebody else's walk with God at midnight. What you have at the moment of the cry is what you brought.

Then the talents, and there is a number worth knowing. A talent was about twenty years of wages for a working man. The servant who got one talent was handed a fortune. That parable is usually read as though he got a little and the others got a lot, and that is not the picture at all.

His problem is not that he lost money. He returns every coin. His problem is that he did nothing, and the reason he gives is fear. And listen to how he describes his master. A hard man. Reaping where he did not sow. That is not the master the other two met. He buried the talent because he believed something untrue about the man who gave it to him.

Then the last scene, and it is not a parable. It is a description, and it is the final thing He teaches before Gethsemane. Sheep and goats grazed together all day in that country and were only separated at evening, which is the point. From the outside they were mixed in together.
And look at the list. Hungry, thirsty, a stranger, naked, sick, in prison. Six things, and not one of them is a religious act. No doctrine is being tested. No attendance. Six ordinary human needs.

Both groups are astonished. Neither one knew. The sheep are not aware they were serving Him and the goats are not aware they were refusing Him. And what the goats are charged with is not cruelty. It is absence. Not what they did. What they did not do.
