chapters.heading: CHAPTER 26 - An Alabaster Jar, a Cup He Asked to Pass, and a Rooster
chapters.title: An Alabaster Jar, a Cup He Asked to Pass, and a Rooster
keyNotes: "When Jesus had finished all these words" closes the fifth and final discourse. The teaching is over; from here it is all narrative (Matthew 26:1).
He names the timing Himself - after two days, the Passover - and names the method: crucified (Matthew 26:2).
The leadership's plan was explicitly not to do it during the feast. They lost control of their own timetable (Matthew 26:5).
The house belongs to Simon the leper - presumably a man He had healed, since a leper could not have hosted anyone (Matthew 26:6).
Anointing the head is what you do to a king. She may have meant one thing; He reads it as burial preparation (Matthew 26:7, 12).
"You always have the poor with you" is a quotation of Deuteronomy 15:11, which commands open generosity - not a dismissal of the poor (Matthew 26:11).
Thirty pieces of silver is the compensation for a gored slave in Exodus 21, and the wage thrown to the potter in Zechariah 11 (Matthew 26:15).
"He who dipped his hand with me in the dish" makes the betrayal a table act - the deepest breach of hospitality there was (Matthew 26:23).
Judas asks "is it me, Rabbi" while the others say "Lord." The title he uses is the one he still means (Matthew 26:25, 22).
The cup is named the blood of the covenant, which is Exodus 24 language, and new covenant, which is Jeremiah 31 (Matthew 26:28).
The hymn they sang was almost certainly the Hallel, ending in Psalm 118 - the psalm the crowd shouted at the entry (Matthew 26:30).
He quotes Zechariah 13:7 about the shepherd struck, and then immediately promises to meet them in Galilee afterward (Matthew 26:31-32).
Gethsemane means oil press. He sweats there under a weight, in a place named for crushing (Matthew 26:36).
"My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death" is Psalm 42 language on His own lips (Matthew 26:38).
He prays the same prayer three times, and the second time the wording shifts from if it is possible to if this cannot pass (Matthew 26:39, 42).
"The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" is said as an excuse for them, not against them (Matthew 26:41).
"Friend, why are you here" - the same courteous word used for the man without a wedding garment (Matthew 26:50, 22:12).
Twelve legions is roughly seventy-two thousand angels - one legion for Him and each of the eleven (Matthew 26:53).
The false witnesses cannot agree, which under Deuteronomy 19 should have ended the trial (Matthew 26:59-60).
He is silent until He is put under oath by the living God, and then He answers plainly and quotes Daniel 7 (Matthew 26:63-64).
Peter's denials escalate: a simple no, then an oath, then cursing. Nobody falls all at once (Matthew 26:70, 72, 74).
Matthew records the weeping but not the restoration; that is left for the end of John (Matthew 26:75).

intro: Verse 1 closes the last of the five great discourses in this Gospel. He has stopped teaching. Everything from here is what happens to Him.

And notice who is in control of the timetable. The chief priests decide explicitly not to act during the feast, because of the crowds. And it happens during the feast anyway. They did not choose the hour. He said in verse 2 exactly when it would be.

The woman with the jar is worth slowing down for. Anointing the head is what you do to a king; Samuel poured oil on David's head. She may well have meant it that way. He receives it as something else: she has prepared my body for burial. She is the only person in the story who does anything for Him in that week, and the disciples call it waste.

And the line often quoted against the poor, you always have the poor with you, is a quotation. It comes from Deuteronomy 15:11, and the rest of that verse commands you to open your hand wide to the poor. He is not dismissing them. He is citing a command about them.

Thirty pieces of silver has a history. In Exodus 21 it is the compensation paid when an ox gores somebody's slave. In Zechariah 11 it is the insulting wage the shepherd is paid and told to throw to the potter. That is what He was priced at.

Then the upper room, and a cup, and words no one in that room could have fully carried: this is my blood of the new covenant. Exodus 24 for the blood of the covenant. Jeremiah 31 for the new one. Two texts, one sentence.

Then Gethsemane, and the name means oil press, the place where olives were crushed under stone weight. He prays three times, and there is a small terrible shift between the first prayer and the second. The first says if it is possible, let this cup pass. The second says if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done. Somewhere between those two He got His answer.

And watch Peter go down in stages. First a flat denial. Then a denial with an oath. Then cursing and swearing. Nobody arrives at the third step directly. And notice that Matthew leaves him weeping in the dark; the restoration is not in this book.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 27 - Thirty Pieces Returned, a Crown of Thorns, and a Curtain Torn from the Top
chapters.title: Thirty Pieces Returned, a Crown of Thorns, and a Curtain Torn from the Top
keyNotes: Judas feels remorse and returns the money, which is not the same as repentance - he goes to the priests rather than to Yahshua (Matthew 27:3-5).
The priests will not put blood money in the treasury but were willing to pay it out of the treasury. The scruple is about the ledger, not the deed (Matthew 27:6).
The potter's field detail draws on Zechariah 11 and on Jeremiah's field purchase and potter imagery; Matthew names Jeremiah (Matthew 27:9-10).
Before Pilate He says three words and then nothing. The governor marvels, which is not a word used lightly of a Roman judge (Matthew 27:11-14).
Barabbas means son of the father. The crowd chooses one son of the father over another (Matthew 27:16-17).
Pilate's wife is the only person in the trial narrative who calls Him righteous (Matthew 27:19).
Pilate washes his hands using a gesture straight out of Deuteronomy 21 - a Jewish rite for disclaiming bloodguilt (Matthew 27:24).
The scarlet robe, the reed sceptre and the thorn crown are a mock coronation. The soldiers are staging a king (Matthew 27:28-29).
Thorns first appear in Genesis 3 as part of the curse on the ground. He wears them (Matthew 27:29).
Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross - a Roman soldier's legal right to conscript a civilian (Matthew 27:32).
He refuses the drugged wine. Whatever is coming, He intends to be conscious for it (Matthew 27:34).
Matthew reports the crucifixion itself in four words - "when they had crucified him" - and spends the space on the psalm being fulfilled around it (Matthew 27:35).
The mockers unknowingly quote Psalm 22:8 almost exactly: he trusts in God, let God deliver him (Matthew 27:43).
Three hours of darkness at midday, from noon to three - the hours of the afternoon sacrifice (Matthew 27:45).
The cry from the cross is the first line of Psalm 22, a psalm that ends in vindication and worldwide worship (Matthew 27:46).
The veil separated the holy place from the most holy. Torn from the top down is a detail about who did the tearing (Matthew 27:51).
The centurion - a Gentile, and the executioner - is the first human being in this Gospel to say it at the cross: truly this was the Son of God (Matthew 27:54).
The women are named and were watching. Matthew is careful to establish who saw the death, the burial and the tomb (Matthew 27:55-56, 61).
Joseph of Arimathaea is rich, and the burial in his new tomb fulfils Isaiah 53:9 exactly - with a rich man in his death (Matthew 27:57-60).
The guard is set at the request of the priests, which means the tomb is sealed and watched by His opponents (Matthew 27:62-66).

intro: Judas is the first thing in this chapter, and the distinction the text makes is precise. He felt remorse. He returned the money. He said the true sentence out loud: I have sinned, I betrayed innocent blood. And then he took it to the priests instead of to Yahshua. Remorse and repentance are not the same road, and one of them ends in a field.

Watch the priests in verse 6, because it is one of the most exact pictures of a certain kind of religion in Scripture. They cannot put the money in the treasury; it is blood money, that would be unlawful. They took it out of the treasury to buy a man's life a day earlier. The scruple is about bookkeeping.

Then Pilate. Notice how little Yahshua says. Three words to the only question that mattered, and then silence, and Matthew reports that the governor marvelled greatly. Roman judges did not marvel at prisoners. And the choice offered to the crowd has an irony sitting in the name: Barabbas means son of the father.

The mock coronation is deliberate. A robe, a reed for a sceptre, a crown; the soldiers are dressing up a king to laugh at. And the crown is made of thorns, which entered the world in Genesis 3 as part of the curse on the ground. He wears the curse on His head.

Then something worth noticing about how Matthew writes verse 35. He does not describe the crucifixion. Four words: when they had crucified him. Every ancient reader knew what that involved and he does not linger. What he spends his words on is what was being fulfilled around it: the garments divided, the lots cast, the heads wagging, the taunt from Psalm 22 coming out of the mouths of men who did not know they were quoting.

And at the ninth hour He cries out the first line of that same psalm. Psalm 22 is worth reading all the way through, because it does not stay where that line leaves it. It ends with all the ends of the earth remembering and turning to Yahweh.

Then the veil. That curtain separated the holy place from the most holy, the place one man entered one day a year. It tore from the top down. Nobody standing on the ground tears anything from the top.

And notice who says the sentence this whole Gospel has been building toward. Not a disciple; they have fled. Not a priest. A Roman centurion, the man in charge of the execution: truly this was the Son of God.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 28 - An Empty Tomb, a Bribed Story, and a Commission That Still Stands
chapters.title: An Empty Tomb, a Bribed Story, and a Commission That Still Stands
keyNotes: The women come after the Sabbath, at dawn. They are not expecting a resurrection; they come to see a grave (Matthew 28:1).
The stone is not rolled away to let Him out but to let them in. He is already gone when it moves (Matthew 28:2, 6).
The angel sits on the stone. It is a posture of completion, not of effort (Matthew 28:2).
The guards, who were there to prevent exactly this, become like dead men - while the dead man is alive (Matthew 28:4).
"Just like he said" is the angel's reproach and comfort in four words. He had told them repeatedly (Matthew 28:6).
Women are the first witnesses, in a culture where a woman's testimony carried little legal weight. No one inventing a story would build it this way (Matthew 28:5-8).
"Fear and great joy" together is one of the most honest descriptions of an encounter with God in Scripture (Matthew 28:8).
He meets them on the road with the ordinary greeting of the day - chairete, rejoice, the everyday hello (Matthew 28:9).
They take hold of His feet. Matthew is quietly establishing that the risen body could be touched (Matthew 28:9).
"Go tell my brothers" is said of men who abandoned Him four days earlier. The word choice is the restoration (Matthew 28:10).
The bribed story is self-defeating - sleeping witnesses cannot testify to what happened while they slept (Matthew 28:13).
The priests promise to protect the soldiers from Pilate, which admits they expect the governor to care (Matthew 28:14).
"Some doubted" is left in the text at the moment of greatest triumph. Matthew does not tidy his own ending (Matthew 28:17).
"All authority has been given to me" is the answer to the wilderness offer of the kingdoms of the world in chapter 4 (Matthew 28:18, 4:8-9).
The commission's main verb is make disciples; going, baptising and teaching are the participles hanging off it (Matthew 28:19).
"All nations" reverses the restriction of chapter 10 - and fulfils the promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed (Matthew 28:19, 10:5-6).
"Teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you" makes obedience, not information, the goal of the teaching (Matthew 28:20).
The book opened with Immanuel, God with us, and closes with I am with you always. The whole Gospel is bracketed by that promise (Matthew 28:20, 1:23).
There is no ascension scene in Matthew. He ends with Yahshua still speaking, still present, the commission unfinished (Matthew 28:20).

intro: They are not coming to see a resurrection. They are coming to see a grave. That matters, because it tells you what everyone expected on that morning, including the people who had heard Him say three times what would happen.

And the stone is a detail worth getting right. It is not moved to let Him out; verse 6 says He was already risen when they arrived. It is moved to let them in, so they could see the place where the Lord was lying. And the angel sits down on it, which is a posture that says the work is over.
Notice the reversal in verse 4. The guards, armed, awake, posted specifically to prevent this, become like dead men. And the dead man is not there.

Then something that has convinced a good many honest sceptics over the years: the first witnesses are women. In that legal culture a woman's testimony carried almost no weight in court. Anyone fabricating a story to persuade first-century people would not build it on witnesses the audience was trained to discount. It is in the text because it is what happened.
And verse 8 is one of the truest sentences in Scripture about meeting God: fear and great joy. Not one or the other. Both, running down the same road.

Then He meets them, and what He says is chairete, the ordinary hello of that world. Good morning, more or less. And they grab His feet, which is Matthew saying quietly that this was a body you could hold on to.
Then verse 10, which is the one not to miss. Go tell my brothers. Four days ago every one of them ran. Peter had sworn on oath that he never knew Him. And the first word He sends them is brothers.

Notice verse 17: they worshipped him, but some doubted. Matthew leaves that in, at the summit of his own book, in the last scene. He does not clean it up. And the commission is given to that group, the worshipping and the doubting together.

And notice how the book closes. It opened in chapter 1 with a name: Immanuel, God with us. It ends with I am with you always, even to the end of the age. There is no ascension in Matthew, no farewell. He is still talking when the book stops.

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 1-3

A legal line running through a cursed king, and a pattern broken at exactly the right verse
Righteousness that looks like a man choosing the quieter way to end an engagement
A name that is a job description - Yahweh saves - and what He saves His people from

The wilderness as the place God keeps starting again
Ancestry dismantled: God can raise children to Abraham out of gravel
Repentance made measurable by what grows out of it
The King baptized among sinners, because standing with them was the fitting way
The throne and the cross named in a single sentence over the water

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 4-6
items: Testing that the Spirit leads into rather than fails to prevent
Israel's wilderness lived over again, and answered every time from the chapter that explains it

Light switched on in the corner of the country that had been dark longest

Six times underneath the commandment to the wanting that produces it
A righteousness that cannot be reached by keeping more rules than the rule-keepers
Religion with the audience removed, and a reward already paid in full to those who wanted one
A prayer whose first half is not about us, prayed in the plural behind a shut door
Forgiveness as the one petition He goes back and presses
The heart following the treasure rather than the other way round

Enough trouble today, and a Kingdom to seek first

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 7-9

Fear addressed before the weather is

A town that preferred its pigs
Somebody else's faith carrying a man who could not walk

Mercy over sacrifice, with the scholars sent to do their homework
Twelve years of bleeding and twelve years of living, healed at the corner of a garment
A shepherd who felt the crowd in his gut, and told them to pray for the labourers they became

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 10-12

A sparrow that still falls, but never unnoticed
A cup of cold water as the last word after swords and crosses
Certainty and doubt living in the same man, and neither one disqualifying him
A question answered in Isaiah's vocabulary, with the one clause John needed left unquoted
Doubt handled in private, reputation defended in public
Judgment measured by light received, falling hardest on His own town
An invitation that arrives immediately after the woes
A yoke offered rather than removed, by the only one who describes His own heart
Mercy over sacrifice, quoted twice in four chapters
One greater than the temple, and Lord of the day itself

A sign demanded straight after a sign, and answered with a prophet in a fish

A house swept clean and left empty, which does not stay empty

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 13-15
items: Stories that sort the people listening rather than making things simpler

An assignment handed to men who had just explained they could not do it
Twelve baskets left over - one apiece for the ones who said it was impossible

A hand that reaches first and asks the question afterward

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 16-18

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 19-21

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 22-24

Watching that turns out to look like feeding the household on time

parts.title: Major Themes Across Matthew 25-28
items: Three parables about a delay, told to men who had asked when
Ten girls alike in everything but one flask of oil, and nobody blamed for sleeping
Readiness that cannot be borrowed at midnight
A fortune buried by a man who believed something untrue about the one who gave it
Sheep and goats grazing together all day and separated only at evening
Six ordinary human needs, and not one religious act among them
Both groups astonished, and the charge against one being absence rather than cruelty
A jar broken by the only person who did anything for Him that week, and called waste
A price with a history: compensation for a slave, an insulting wage thrown to a potter
Two texts in one sentence - the blood of the covenant, and the covenant made new
A garden named for crushing, and a prayer that changes wording between the first time and the second
A man who went down in three stages, and a book that leaves him weeping
Remorse that went to the priests instead of to Him
A scruple about the treasury from men who had just bought a life out of it
Thorns from the curse in Genesis, worn on His head
A crucifixion reported in four words, and a psalm quoted by men who did not know they were quoting
A curtain torn from the top down, which is a detail about who did the tearing
The confession of the whole Gospel spoken by the executioner
A stone moved to let them in rather than to let Him out
First witnesses that no inventor of a story would have chosen
Fear and great joy running down the same road
The word brothers, sent to men who had all run
Worship and doubt in the same room, and the commission given to both
A book that opens with God with us and ends with I am with you always
